notes: A pronominal prefix, most likely the neuter singular pronoun “it”, appearing in the word ayadda “[it] went” in the sentence “the road west [it] once went straight” (SD/247). See the entry on for more discussion.

An element in the name , whose Quenya equivalent seems to mean “*World Tower” (UT/222). Since the last element of this name is “pillar”, it is possible that the first element means “world”. This first element could be *abat, but it could also be *aban with the last n becoming t according to the Adûnaic rules for , as suggested before by several authors (/9, /BAN¹). Andreas Moehn further suggested () it may have replaced earlier “Earth”, though the two words could also co-exist with slightly different meanings.

A noun translated as “strength, endurance, fidelity”, and used as an example of noun declension in Lowdham’s Report (SD/431). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/9) that it may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “endure”. It may also be related to the name “*Steadfast, Faithful”.

Conceptual Development: This word also appeared in earlier Adûnaic names and (both glossed “Land of Gift”), where it apparently had the meaning “gift”. These names were eventually replaced by in which the element means “gift”, freeing abâr to have the meaning: “strength, endurance, fidelity”.

The Adûnaic name of the Tar-, the 19th rulers of Númenor (UT/222). His Quenya name appears to mean “*World Tower”. The last element of his Adûnaic name is clearly Ad. “pillar”, so perhaps its meaning is similar. If so, the first element of his Adûnaic name may mean “World”. Andreas Moehn suggested (/BAN¹) this element is likely * or abân, with the final n altered to t in the compound according to the rules of Adûnaic .

The Adûnaic name that Lowdham used to address Jeremy in Tolkien’s unfinished story: “The Notion Club Papers” (SD/252). In an earlier version of the story, Jeremy was called ᴹQ. (SD/290) and Abrazân may be the Adûnaic equivalent of that name, meaning “Steadfast, Faithful”. If so, its first element is probably related to Ad. “strength, endurance, fidelity”. Andreas Moehn suggested (/BAR) that the entire name may be the of an unattested verb *abrazâ- “to stand fast”.

A prepositional suffix variously translated as “(in)to” or “(to)ward”, and in one place “against” (SD/247, SD/429). It can appears as either -ada or -ad (SD/429), but in most examples it is -ada, the one exception being “Starwards”.

There were two men with this name in Tolkien’s legendarium. Adrahil I was a Gondorian prince who fought with King against the Wainriders (UT/293-4, 319 note #39). Adrahil II was the 21st prince of and the father of (LotR/1056, PM/223). Since Tolkien said that “Imrahil is a Númenórean name” (LotR/1113), it is likely Adrahil was also Adûnaic. It seems that Adûnaic names were traditional for the princes of : many of the known names (such as Adrahil, and ) are Adûnaic in form. It is not clear what the elements of these names might mean, however.

Conceptual Development: In the drafts of the Lord of the Rings appendices, Tolkien listed Adrahil as a Lemberin (Nandorin) name, along with Imrahil (PM/36). Probably when Imrahil became Adûnaic, Adrahil switched languages as well.

A noun meaning “west(ward)” (SD/435, PE17/18). Tolkien stated that was “a loan word from Eldarin speech in the language of the Folk of Hador, from which Númenórean was later derived” (PE17/18). Probably it is derived from S. “west”, as suggested by several authors (/9, /NDU). Tolkien stated that it was an adjective and its proper noun form was (SD/435), but adûn was used as a noun in phrases such as Bârîm an-adûn “Lords of the West” (SD/247).

The Adûnaic word for the Númenóreans themselves, clearly related to “west” (PE17/18, SD/240). It is attested only in plural forms Adûnâi (normal plural) and Adûnâim (subjective plural). The final vowel of its singular form must be a long â; if it were short, its plural form would be **Adûnî instead of the attested Adûnâi.

Son of Ar- and the 20th ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was . In both languages, his name (somewhat heretically) means “Lord of the West” (LotR/1036, S/267). Its first element means “west”, which implies that its second element means “lord”, but it isn’t clear whether this element is *akhôr or *. I think that khôr is more likely, because it resembles the Primitive Elvish root √ “rule, govern, possess”, to which it may be related.

The language of Númenor, appearing in a 1965 document first published in Nature of Middle-earth in 2021 (NM/323). Prior to that point, various hypothetical words have been proposed for this language’s name, such as *Adûnaiyê (Andreas Moehn, ), *Adûnâyê (Thorsten Renk, /1), and Adûnâiyê (my own invention), modelled after “Elvish”.
According to Tolkien, this is the proper noun form of the adjective “west” (SD/435), though adûn is used as a noun in some examples as well.

gloss: [the] road west once went straight, (lit.) west straight road once went
notes:
The 11th phrase of the (SD/247), whose word order varied considerably in the different drafts of the text. The first two words are the adjectives “west” and “straight, right, true”. They modify the subject “road, path, way”, which is in the rather than the . This is consistent with the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, since the verb ayadda has a pronominal suffix a- “*it” (SD/429).

The fourth word is an adverb “once, then”. The verb form yadda seems to be the tense of # “to go”, functioning here as a pluperfect (see SD/439). This makes sense in the narrative, since this sentence describes the previous state (the road west going straight to Valinor) while the next sentence uses the aorist tense to describe the current state (all roads being bent around the now-round world).

Tolkien’s glosses match the word order of the Adûnaic sentence: “west straight road once went”. This might be rendered in more ordinary English as “[the] road west once went straight”.

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence had more differences from the final version than any other sentence in the second draft (SD/312). It had a different word order, with the adjective “straight” appearing directly before the verb, perhaps functioning as an adverb. It has ēluk instead of and the verb form yadda is missing the pronominal prefix a-. Unfortunately, Christopher Tolkien did not publish the English glosses for this sentence, so it is hard to decipher the meaning (if any) of these differences.

The first draft of the 11th phrase of the (SD/312). It resembles the final version, but is missing the adverb and has the verb “to lie” instead of “to go”.

The first two words adūn “west” and batān “road” are the same as in the final version. The verb form akhaini “lay” seems to be the tense of the verb # “to lie”. The word ezendi “straight” (instead of later ) appears at the end, perhaps functioning as an adverb.
The masculine personification of “death” (SD/426). This could be the Adûnaic name for .
A noun for “death” attested both as an independent word (SD/426) and in the compound agannâlô “death-shadow” (SD/247).

The 9th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject agannâlô “death-shadow” is a compound of “death” and “shadow” in the case. The next word “heavy” is simply an adjective, and nênud “on us” is a combination of the pronoun “us” and the prepositional suffix “on”. Since there is no verb, the subjective here functions as the verb “to be” (SD/429), so that the English translation should be “the death-shadow is heavy on us”, though Tolkien did not include “is” in his translation.

In the previous (second draft) version of this sentence, the spelling of some words were slightly different: buruda (as it was in the first draft) instead of the final form burôda and nēnu instead of the final form nēnud (SD/312). The first draft of this sentence uses the same words but is grammatically different.

The first draft of the 9th phrase of the (SD/312), which was close to the final version but had minor differences in spelling and grammar. The subject agannūlo “death-shade” seems to be in the rather than the , and nūlo “shade” is a variant spelling of later . The word burudan “heavy” seems to buruda (so spelled in the second draft but in the final version) with the predicate suffix “is”. The final word nēnum “on us” is a combination of the pronoun “us” and the prepositional suffix -num “on” (nēnu in the second draft and nēnud in the final version).

The Adûnaic name of the river S. “Greyflood” (UT/263), also glossed “flood under shadow” (VT42/9). This later name does not fit the Adûnaic phonetic rules described by Tolkien in Lowdham’s Report, since “sh” [ʃ] is not a phoneme used in Adûnaic (SD/418). It may be that Tolkien changed his mind about the phonemes of Adûnaic, or it may be that Agathurush had already undergone some of the phonetic changes leading to the Westron language, which had this sound (LotR/1120). It isn’t clear how this name could be decomposed into its elements.

The 19th prince of (PM/223). The language and meaning of this name are not clear, but based on the idea that the princes of Dol Amroth took Adûnaic names (as discussed in the entry for ), this entry assumes the name is Adûnaic. David Salo attempted to analyze it as a Sindarin name instead (GS/340).
An element of the name that might be a noun meaning “glory”; see the entry for that name for further discussion.

An earlier name for the ship , likely the Adûnaic equivalent of that name (SD/372, PM/156). Aglarrâma was glossed “Castle of the Sea”, but many students of Tolkien’s languages feel that this is unlikely to be a literal translation of the name. The first part of its Quenya name is Q. “glory”, and the element Ad. of its Adûnaic name may have the same meaning, possibly as a loan word from S. . It is not clear what the last element of the name would mean. This analysis is all rather speculative, since it isn’t even clear what languages the names Aglarrâma and Alcarondas belong to.

A suffix in the word “far away”, a derivative of “far” (SD/247). Some authors have suggested that -ak is an intensive suffix “very” instead of suffix meaning “away” (, /32). However, the corresponding Quenya word “far away” is a combination “(away) from” and “far”, so it seems to me that the literal translation “away” is more likely to be correct (this translation of va was published after and were written).

The Adûnaic name of Númenor after its fall, the equivalent of Q. (S/281). Tolkien usually translated this word as “Downfallen”, but its literal meaning was “(She) That Has Fallen” (PE17/111, SD/247). The final element seems to be a feminine suffix, also seen in . The middle element -kallab- seems to be the past formation kallaba of the verb “to fall (down)”. The function of the initial a- isn’t clear, but it may be some sort of perfective augment, as seen in the Quenya tense; see the discussion of the Adûnaic for more information.

Other Interpretations: Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/36) that the prefix a- is probably some kind of emphatic suffix rather than evidence of another verb tense. Thorsten Renk proposes (/39) that the a- is a relative pronoun “that”, analogous to Q. , which is an interesting possibility.
A noun for “chasm” attested only in the prepositional phrase akhāsada “into chasm” (SD/247) and akhās-ada “chasm-into” (SD/311), the latter example making it clear which element means what.

The Adûnaic name of (SD/376). According to Christopher Tolkien, the invention of this Adûnaic name preceded the use of Q. as the name of the Blessed Realm, and was likely the inspiration for this Quenya name (SD/376). The later status of Ad. Amân as the name of Manwë is unclear, but it could be that the ancestors of the Númeróreans conflated the name of the Valar with the name of the land he ruled.

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name for Manwë was (SD/55).
A draft version of the Adûnaic name for , later replaced by (SD/376).

The primitive form of , the Adûnaic name of Manwë, written in allcaps as AMĀN (SD/420). Usually Tolkien used capitalization for primitive roots, but in this case it is more like to be a form derived from an unattested Primitive Adûnaic root *√MAN, probably related to the Primitive Elvish root ᴹ√.

The Adûnaic name for the Blessed Realm, home of the Valar (SD/388, SD/420). Its Quenya equivalent would be , though Tolkien did not coin the Quenya name until a later conceptual stage of his legendarium. The Adûnaic word is derived from their name for the ruler of the Bless Realm: (Manwë). Its literal meaning is “Manwë’s Land”.

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name for the Blessed Realm was (SD/385).

A draft Adûnaic name for the Blessed Realm, later replaced by (SD/385). Its initial element is a draft name for “land” also seen in the draft name “Land of Gift”. Its final element is , the Adûnaic name of Manwë, joined to the first element with an elided form of the genitive prefix “of”. Therefore, the literal meaning of the name is “Land of Amân (Manwë)”.

A noun for “mother” (SD/434). Tolkien gave two forms of this word, ammî and ammê, with no indication as to which would be preferred. However, ammî resembles a plural word, and Tolkien elsewhere stated that such forms tended to change their final vowel to -ê (SD/438), so my guess is that ammî is an archaic form. This word is probably related to the Elvish root √ “mother”. Some authors have suggested it is directly related to ᴹQ. (/10, /Adûnaic), but as Andreas Moehn points out (/MAM) such basic words are rarely borrowed from other languages, so the relationship is more likely from the Primitive Elvish root.

A noun translated “human being” (SD/426) given as an example of a noun ending in a long vowel that (archaically) uses the declension for a (SD/437), an example of the extremely rare class of Strong-IIb nouns. By the time of Classical Adûnaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead. It also had masculine and feminine variants anû “(human) man” and anî “(human) woman” (SD/434) but in ordinary speech it seems likely that more specific words would be used: “man, male”, “female”, “woman”.

The Adûnaic name for Númenor (Q. ), with the same meaning as its Quenya name: “Westernesse” (S/261). In The Silmarillion appendix, Christopher Tolkien stated that is it a loan word from Elvish (SA/andúnë). According to J.R.R. Tolkien’s own writing (SD/426), this is true, albeit not directly. Anadûnê is a feminized form of the adjective “western, of the west”, which is itself related to S. “west”.

The 6th phrase of the (SD/247). Its subject “Númenor” is in the rather than the . This is consistent with the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, which allowed a normal subject if the verb has a pronominal inflection (SD/429), in this case the prefix hi- “she” of the verb hikalba (place names in Adûnaic are often ).

The placement of the adjective “beloved” after the noun is curious, since according to Tolkien adjectives normally precede the nouns they modify (SD/428). Perhaps in this instance the adjective is used as a noun. Its manuscript gloss “the beloved” instead of simply “beloved” (as in the typescript) supports this possibility. Alternately, it could be in an abnormal position because it is a (verbal adjective).

The verbs in the typescript and manuscript versions are slightly different: kallaba “fell down” (SD/247) and kalba “fell” (VT24/12), the and tenses of the verb “to fall (down)”. Tolkien also vacillated between these two forms in the second draft version of the sentence before settling on the aorist. Since the fall of Númenor had already come to pass in the fictional context of the Lament, the past tense here could be functioning here as a pluperfect (SD/439), but the aorist tense would also work if the sentence describes the fall of Númenor at that point in the narrative. Tolkien’s vacillation is therefore understandable: either verb form could work albeit with slightly different meanings. The Quenya translation of this sentence, ᴹQ. (SD/247), uses the simple past instead of the perfect, matching the Adûnaic manuscript version rather than typescript.

The first draft of the 6th phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version in its grammar and in the omission of the word “beloved”. The subject anadūni seems to be an earlier version of “Númenor”. The verb akallabi “fell in ruin” is an early form of “to fall (down)”, perhaps in the tense.

An adjective translated “western” formed from the noun “the West” which was in turn formed from the adjective “west”; the initial was the genitival prefix (SD/435). This adjective anadûni was in turn femininized to produce the place name “Westeresse, Númenor”.

The 20th prince of (PM/223). The language and meaning of this name are not clear, but based on the idea that the princes of Dol Amroth took Adûnaic names (as discussed in the entry for ), this entry assumes the name is Adûnaic. David Salo suggested instead it was Sindarin (GS/341).
An element of the name (SD/389), possibly meaning “bliss”; see the entry for that name for further discussion.

The Adûnaic name for Q. (SD/389). The last element of this name is an for the verb “to love”, also seen in the name of his son “Elf-friend” (Q. ). The initial element seems to be the form of a noun , whose meaning is unclear. The equivalent element in his Quenya name is “Blessed Realm”, but Tolkien had not yet coined this word when he invented the name Aphanuzîr. Andreas Moehn suggested (/PHAN) that it means “bliss”. This fits the earlier story of the Lost Road (LR), in which Tolkien wrote of various incarnations of a father and son whose names were “Bliss-friend” and “Elf-friend” in many languages. Amandil and Elendil were two of these incarnations.

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name given to this character was (SD/365).
The draft name for . Tolkien may have changed the name because of its similarity to “*Steadfast, Faithful”.

The Adûnaic name for the capital of Númenor, whose Quenya name is (SD/363, PM/145). The final element seems to be a feminizing suffix, also seen in Ad. . The initial element is the same as that used in the name of kings and queens, and the middle element means “heaven”, so perhaps the literal meaning is something like *“Royal Heaven (City)”, similar in the sense to the Quenya name.
A short phrase illustrating the Adûnaic compositional (SD/435).

A phrase given by Tolkien as an example of how a pair of nouns would be declined into the case, with only the last noun inflected (SD/429). The entire noun phrase would be the subject of the sentence. It is contrasted with , where the first noun is inflected instead. This would be a the sentences “Ar-Pharazôn (is) a conquerer”.

The 3rd phrase of the (SD/247). It differed from its earlier drafts only in its use of grammar. Tolkien’s gloss was “‽ was warring against Powers”, omitting the name Ar-Pharazôn because Lowdham was unsure how to translate it. In more ordinary English might be “Ar-Pharazôn was warring against the Powers”.

The subject Ar-Pharazônun is the form of the name Ar-. The verb azaggara “was warring” is a form of “to wage war”, either the past tense or continuative-past tense (see the entry for that tense for further discussion). The last word Avalôiyada “against the Powers” is the plural form of “Power, God” with the prepositional suffix “toward, against” separated from the i of the plural by the usual y.

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence differs from the final version in two ways (SD/312). First, the subject is in the instead of the case, perhaps because Tolkien had not finalized the rules for the subjective case. Second, its verb form was azagrāra, although the final verb form azaggara was written nearby as an alternative. See the verb for possible interpretations.

The first draft of the 3rd phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version primarily in grammar. It has a difficult-to-interpret form azgaranādu of the verb . See the entry to that verb for possible interpretations. The last word avalōi-si seems to be the plural form of “Power, God”, changed from the plural form avalōi-men.

gloss: King Pharazon is Lord of Anadune
notes: An example sentence illustrating Adûnaic grammar: it is a copula (a “to be” expression) without an explicit verb for “is” (SD/428). The subject of the sentence, Ar-Pharazônun, is in the case, which represents the verb “to be”. The rest of the sentence, Bâr ’nAnadûnê “Lord of Anadune (Númenor)” is the predicate and is in the . This sentence also provides an example of the use of the genitive prefix “of”, here elided to ’n because of the preceding uninflected noun.

A phrase given by Tolkien as an example of how the case can be used to represent the verb “to be” (SD/429). Since the first noun the subject, the second noun is the predicate and the verb “is” is implied. Depending on context, the sentenced could refer to the past so that the subjective would represent “was” instead. This sentence is contrasted with , where the second noun is inflected in the subjective instead, so that the entire noun phrase would be the subject: “King Ar-Pharazon the Conqueror...”.
A noun translated as “king” (SD/429). The Adûnaic word for “queen” is not attested, but could be a feminized form of this word, such as *ârî.

An Adûnaic name for Morgoth, perhaps coined by Sauron when he introduced the worship of the dark god to the Númenóreans, translated as “Lord” (SD/376). It is derived from the word “king” and was sometimes used in a compound together with Morgoth’s true Adûnaic name: Arûn- (SD/367). In other writings (SD/357) it was the original Adûnaic name of Morgoth before he fell to evil, but that hardly makes sense in the conceptual scenario of the later Silmarillion, in which Morgoth had already become evil before men awoke.

A rejected draft version of the Adûnaic name for Morgoth translated “Lord”, replaced by of the same meaning (SD/376). It is transparently a derivative of the Elvish root ᴹ√, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/18). A later form of this word, * “lord”, may appears as an element in the name “Lord of the West”.

An phrase illustrating Adûnaic grammar, in particular how the genitive prefix “of” must be used when a plural noun needs to be put into a genitive relationship with another noun (SD/429). Without the an-, the preceding noun would be in an relationship instead. Here the an- is elided to ’n because of the preceding uninflected noun.

An otherwise unexplained root Tolkien gave to illustrate a pronunciation example (SD/421). It may not be a real root. If it is real, it is either a <a l="pad" v="biconsonantal-root"/> with <a l="pad" v="vowel-prefixion"/> or a <a l="pad" v="triconsonantal-root"/> with a lost initial consonant such as <a l="pad" v="[ɣ]"/> or <a l="pad" v="[ʔ]"/>.
A word Tolkien used to illustrate Adûnaic pronunciation (pronounced [azdi]) without giving its meaning (SD/421).

A noun for “father” (SD/434). Tolkien gave two forms of this word, attû and attô, with no indication as to which would be preferred. For reasons similar to those given in the entry for “mother”, my guess is that attû is an archaic form, and attô was preferred by the time of Classical Adûnaic. This word is probably related to the Elvish root √ “father”, perhaps from Primitive Elvish ᴹ✶.
The feminine form of “God, Power”, translated “Goddess” (SD/428). Like its masculine equivalent, it is probably pronounced [awalē], since the sound in Adûnaic was sometime written “v” (SD/434).

The Adûnaic name for , though it may also (or instead) have referred the Blessed Realm, home of the Valar (SD/241). It was translated “Haven of the Gods” (SD/361). Given its meaning, the name seems to contain the word Ad. , the Adûnaic name for the Valar. It seems likely that Ad. Avallôni is direct borrowing of Q. “Outer Isle”, reinterpreted by the Númenorieans to fit their language. It is probably pronounced [awallōni], since the sound in Adûnaic was sometime written “v” (SD/434).

Conceptual Development: An earlier form of this name, Avallondē may have been a mixed name, containing the Quenya element ᴹQ. (SD/344).

An Adûnaic noun translated as “God” or “Power” (SD/247, 305), the equivalent of (and possibly derived from) Q. . It is probably pronounced [awalō], since the sound in Adûnaic was sometime written “v” (SD/434). It frequently appeared in its plural or subjective plural forms Avalôi(m) “Powers, Gods”.

Conceptual Development: In early drafts of Adûnaic its plural was Avalâi with a long â instead of ô, perhaps indicating an earlier singular form Avalâ closer to Vala. Earlier still this word was given as plural Balāi, a more direct derivative of the Elvish root form ᴹ√.
An earlier version of the Adûnaic word for Q. (SD/344), later replaced by Avalâi >> Avalôi. It is only attested in its plural form Balâi.

An Adûnaic name for a goddess with the title “Star-kindler” (SD/428). Though Tolkien never made it explicit, it is clearly the Adûnaic name of (S. ). This name is curious, since [v] is not one of the phonemes used in Adûnaic (SD/418). Most likely it is pronounced [awradī]. Tolkien said that to represent the sound , he sometimes “used ‘v’ in the Anglicanizing of Adunaic names” (SD/434). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/12) that it may be a derivative of Primitive Elvish ✶.

A hypothetical noun for “war” appearing as an element in the verb “to wage war”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/24), though as others have suggested (/Adûnaic, /ZAG’R) it could equally well be azgar.

A verb meaning “to wage war” (SD/439), one of two examples of an and the only one with any attested inflections. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne initially suggested it is composed of the words * “war” and a causative suffix * (/24), but later suggested (/12) it may be related * so that its literal meaning was “*wield a weapon” or “*put to the sword”, similar to ᴹQ. “wield a weapon, fight” < ᴹ√ “sword”. Andreas Moehn also suggested (/ZAG’R) the verb may be related to * “sword”.

This verb appears in slightly different forms in each version of the , changing as follows: azgaranādu (SD/311) >> azagrāra (SD/312) >> azaggara (SD/247). All three versions have similar glosses, “was waging war” or “was warring”, which seems to imply these are all instances of the tense. As they are the only clear instances of this tense, it is difficult to decipher the conceptual development of this verb.

The first form azgaranādu belongs to the draft Adûnaic period and is probably grammatically distinct from the later forms. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne thoroughly analyzed this draft form (/35). The two later forms appeared in very similar versions of the Lament. Rather than representing a revision of the grammar, they could represent distinct verb tenses, as for example Tolkien’s vacillation between the forms hikalba and hikallaba in the sentence . The question is, to which tense does each form belong?

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/28) concluded that the azaggara represents the without analyzing azagrāra. Andreas Moehn agreed with them in his grammatical article on Adûnaic () but changed his mind in his etymological analysis (/ZAG’R), concluding it is the past tense instead. I also believe azaggara is more likely to be a simple past tense.

The double-g of the form azaggara resembles other verb forms identified as the tense in the theories used here, and it seems likelier to me that Tolkien changed the verb from the continuative-past to the simple past without revising the gloss. The second a in azaggara is likely inserted in the verb stem to break up the consonant cluster in az-ggara, since Adûnaic allows at most two consecutive (SD/418).

If the above reasoning is correct, this would make the form azagrāra the best candidate for the continuative-past. Perhaps the repetition of the final suffix -ra is used to mark the continuous nature of the action. All of this is highly speculative, however, since we are working only from a single example.
The Adûnaic word for “sea” (SD/429), appearing as azar in some early texts (SD/305). It is fully declined on SD/431.
A draft word for “sea”, deleted and replaced with azar (SD/305), which later become . This word reappeared later with a different meaning: “gold”.
A noun given as an example of a <a l="ad" v="genitive"/> compound (SD/429), translated “sea-lands, maritime regions” (SD/435) but literally meaning “*lands of the sea”.

gloss: that [the] seas should gush into [the] chasm
notes:
The 5th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject azrîya is the plural of “sea”. Judging by the glosses, the verbal prefix most likely indicates the or moods (see those entries for discussion). The verb form phursâ resembles the tense of the verb , except that the long â is unusual. Perhaps this variation is because the verb is actually in an infinitive form, though Andreas Moehn instead suggested the verb stem may be a derived verb *phursâ- (/PHUR). The last word akhâsada is the word “chasm” with the prepositional suffix “towards, into”.

The gloss of the manuscript version was “that seas should gush into Chasm” (VT24/12). This gloss seems to indicate that this sentence might actually be a subordinate phrase of the preceding sentence “Lords of the West, they broke the Earth with assent from Eru”. This would fit well with its use of the optative/subjunctive mood, so that this phrase gives reason why the Valar broke the Earth (to sink Númenor). However, both the manuscript and typescript versions separated the two sentences with an ellipsis “...”, indicating that they are separate sentences.

The first draft of the 5th phrase of the (SD/311). Its has the same vocabulary as the final version except that it has “might” (an adverb?) instead of the prefix . This nai is almost certainly a variant of Q. “maybe, be it that”.

The draft version has several other grammatical differences from later versions. The subject azrē “seas” seems to be a simple rather than plural. Tolkien initially wrote phurusam for the verb and then changed to phurrusim “flow”, perhaps and tenses of the verb , respectively. Both conjugations have the plural verb suffix . The last phrase akhās-ada “into Chasm” is essentially identical to the final version, however.

The Adûnaic name of Q. , having a similar meaning “Friend of the Sea” (SD/359). The first element is the form of “sea” and the second is an for the verb stem (PM/373). An earlier version of this name, Azrabêl, predates Tolkien’s invention the objective case for Adûnaic (SD/359).

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name given to this character was (SD/305).

The first version of the Adûnaic name of Q. (SD/305), quickly rejected and replaced by Azrabêl, later . Its rejected elements have the same meaning as Azrubêl. Interestingly, the suffix -zîr “-lover” reappeared in the later names and , though as derivations of instead of iri-. The word also reappeared later with the meaning “gold”.
A noun for “east” attested only in the prepositional phrase azûlada “eastward, *to the east” = azûl + “to(ward)” (SD/247, 312).

A particle glossed “don’t” in the phrase “Don’t touch me!”. It may be a derivative of the Elvish root ᴹ√ “refuse, deny, say no”, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (/Adûnaic). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/25, /13) it is an example of the mood mentioned by Tolkien SD/439, where “optative” is an expression of a desire or wish. If so, it expresses a negative wish. A positive wish might be expressed by the particle .

An isolated Adûnaic sentences appearing in “The Notion Club Papers” (SD/250). None of its elements appear elsewhere, making it difficult to interpret, but there is a some consensus in the literature as to the likeliest interpretations. The first word, “don’t” could be derived from the Primitive Elvish root √ “refuse, deny”, possibly an example of the mood (, ). The first element of the second word could be a pronoun ki- “you”. The middle portion tabda could be the aorist form of a verb * “touch”. The last element -hê seems to be the object pronoun “me”, though Thorsten Renk (/18) suggested it is an imperative marker instead.

The noun for “ship”, attested only in the plural (balîk) and objective (balku) forms (SD/247, PM/151). Its plural form indicates that it is a (Strong I), so its final vowel must be short. In theory its final vowel could be any of a, i or u, each of which would be replaced by long î in . However, its attested form uses the variant objective-with-syncope form balku instead of ordinary *baluk. Since the Adûnaic seems only to occur for nouns with two identical short vowels, this indicates the singular form of this word is balak.

The 8th phrase of the (SD/247). As written, it seems to be an incomplete noun phrase rather then a full sentence. It contains neither a verb nor a noun in the case that could represent a copula (“to be” statement).

The first word, balîk “ships” is the normal plural of # “ship”. It is in a composition with the number “seven”, a construction discussed on SD/428, literally meaning “*seven of ships”. This is modified by the phrase an-Nimruzîr “of Elendil” consisting of the genitive prefix “of” and the name (Q. ). The final word, azûlada “eastward(s)” is a composition of “east” and the suffix “(to)wards”.

The final typescript and manuscript versions differ only in that the manuscript is missing the dash “-” in the genitive an-Nimruzîr “of Elendil” (VT24/12). The previous (second draft) version of the phrase is missing the entire prefix an- (SD/312). The first draft had a rather different sentence.

The first draft of the 8th phrase of the (SD/312), which is essentially a different sentence from the final version. The first word Adūnāim is the subjective plural of “Númenórean”. The second word, azūlada “eastwards” is the same as in the final version: a composition of “east” and the suffix “(to)wards”.

The 12th ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- “Shipbuilder, Shipwright” (PM/151). The first element of his name is the form of “ship”. Therefore, the second element most likely means “wright, *builder”. This name appears only in a draft list of the kings of Númenor from the early 1950s, and falls between the conceptual periods of Middle Adûnaic and Late Adûnaic in the terminology used here.

The noun for “wife”, given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a (SD/437), an example of the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns. By the time of Classical Adûnaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead.

A noun translated as “lord” (SD/311, 428). This nouns wins the prize for “most inflected Adûnaic noun”, since we have declensions for this noun in both the draft Adûnaic grammar and the later grammar of Lowdham’s Report. As such, it is very helpful for comparing how the noun declensions changed as Tolkien developed Adûnaic grammar. For example, comparing its draft plurals bāri/bārim to its later plural bârî/bârîm indicate the draft plural was originally formed with a short rather than long i. There are a few lingering examples of this short-i plural in later writings (SD/247, 251).

Conceptual Development: In earlier writings the rejected name “Lord” (SD/376) indicates a possible earlier form of this noun; Kherû itself was changed to . A similar form reappears in later writings in the name “Lord of the West”: either akhôr or “lord”. Whether or not this later word replaced bâr is unknown.

v: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô
gloss: Lords of [the] West, they rent [the] Earth with assent from Eru
notes:
The 4th phrase of the (SD/247). One major conceptual change from earlier versions was that the subject of the sentence was plural Bârim an-Adûn (“Lords of the West”) instead of the earlier singular Bârun an-Adûn (“Lord of the West”). It seems that Tolkien decided that the drowning of Númenor was attributed to all of the Valar rather than just Manwë. A similar change from singular to plural was made in the corresponding Quenya sentence: herunūmen >> númeheruvi.

The subject Bârim of this sentence is the plural of “lord”. It is modified by the adjectival phrase an-Adûn “of the West”, with the genitive prefix “of” added to the noun . The verb has the 3rd-plural suffix yu- “they”. In the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report this makes the subject emphatic, with a meaning more like “It was the Lords of the West who broke the Earth...” (SD/429).

The verb form rahtam is the tense of “to break” with the verb plural suffix . The object of the sentence, “Earth”, is in the .

The base sentence is modified by the prepositional phrase sâibêth-mâ Êruvô “with assent from Eru”. The combination sâibêth-mâ is the word “assent” and the prepositional suffix “with”. The final word Êruvô is the name and the prepositional suffix “of”, with the usual (which was sometimes written “v” as mentioned on SD/434) between the u and the following suffix.

v: bārun an-adūn {urahhata >>} urahta dāira sāibēth-mā ēruvō
notes: The second draft of the 4th phrase of the (SD/312). The key difference between it and final version is that its subject is singular (Manwë only) rather than plural (all of the Valar). Thus, it uses the singular Bârun rather than the later plural Bârim and the pronoun suffix u- “he” instead of later yu- “they”. In this version, Tolkien initially wrote a tense form of the verb rahhata before replacing it with the form rahta used in the final version.

gloss: the Lord of West broke asunder earth assent-with of God
notes:
The first draft of the 4th phrase of the (SD/311). It differs considerably from the final version:

  • The subject is singular “Lord” rather than plural “Lords”, as is the case with the second draft as well.
  • The adjectival phrase adūnō “of the West” uses the case instead of the later genitive prefix .
  • The verb form is rakkhatū, perhaps the draft tense of an early version rakhat- of the verb . It later changed >> urahhata >> urahta >> yurahta. It is glossed “broke asunder” rather than simply “broke” as in later versions.
  • The word for “Earth” is rather than later .
  • In the final phrase sōbēthumā eruvō “assent-with of God”, the two words are likely declined into the and cases, respectively.

An example sentence showing how the can sometimes be used for the subject of a sentence (SD/429). The subject is “lord” while the verb has the masculine singular pronoun prefix u- “he”. Such a prefix is required when the subject is in the normal case (SD/429). The verb form kallaba is the tense of “to fall”. This sentence is contrasted with in which the subject is in the case.

gloss: the lord fell, it was the lord who fell
notes: An example sentence showing how the case is used for the subject of sentences (SD/429). The subject bârun “lord” is the subjective form of . The verb form kallaba is the tense of “to fall”. The masculine singular pronoun prefix u- “he” is optional, but when present makes the sentence emphatic: “it was the lord who fell” (SD/429). This sentence is contrasted with in which the subject is instead in the , which makes the pronoun u- required rather than optional (but not emphatic).
A hypothetical verb, perhaps meaning “walk”, that may appear as an element in the noun “road, path, way”.

A noun variously translated as “road”, “path” or “way” (SD/247, 431; VT24/12) and fully declined on SD/431. This noun also appears in the variant strong-plural form batîn that was sometimes used with Weak I nouns in older and poetic writing (SD/247, 435). Its ordinary weak plural form batânî appears in the declension chart on SD/431. Several authors have suggested (/13, /BAT) that this noun may be a derivative of the Elvish root ᴹ√ “tread” (Ety/BAT). If so, its final element may be the agental suffix , and its initial element may be a verb * “walk”, so that the literal sense of the word might be “*walkway”.

The noun for “wind”, attested only in the plural (bawîb) and subjective plural (bawîba) forms (SD/247, SD/312). Its plural form indicates that it is a (Strong I), so its final vowel must be short, but in theory it could be any of a, i or u, each of which would be replaced by long î in . Nouns with identical vowels are more common, however, so *bawab is the most likely singular form, though as Helge Fauskanger points out (/Adûnaic) the normal form could also be the weak noun *bawâb with a poetic strong plural (SD/435).

The 7th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject bawîba is the plural of # “wind”. There is no verb, so the subjective here functions as the to-be verb “were”, as discussed on SD/429. The adjective dulgî is the plural of “black”, agreeing in number with the subject.

This sentence did not appear at all in the first draft. In the second draft of the Lament, it was simply the noun phrase dulgu bawīb “*black wind” rather than a full sentence (SD/312). Curiously, the adjective in the second draft did not agree in number with the noun it modified.

This unglossed root appears only as an element in the name “Friend of the Sea, Sea-lover” (SD/305). It has a sense similar to that of ✶Ad. √ “love, desire”. Perhaps it is distinct from ✶Ad. √ZIR in that it has more to do with friendship than desire. It could be distantly related to the elvish root √, perhaps ✶mel- > ✶mbel- > ✶bel- in the Avari tongue that influenced Primitive Adûnaic, but this is purely speculative.

This root also contradicts statements by Tolkien elsewhere that Primitive Adûnaic only had the vowels a, i and u. Perhaps it should be *BIL, as with ✶Ad. √ “say” the primitive root of Ad. “expression, saying, word”.
A rejected Adûnaic root attested as iri- and having to do with love (SD/305), perhaps related to the Primitive Elvish root ᴹ√ “desirable, beautiful”.

A verb stem bel- attested only in the explanations for the -bêl in the name “Friend of the Sea, Sea-lover” (SD/305, PM/373). The form bel- violates Adûnaic phonetic rules given in Lowdham’s Report, which state that can only be a long vowel in Adûnaic (SD/423). See the discussion of its root form ✶Ad. √ for possible explanations. The Classical Adûnaic verb form might be bêl-, while bel- may instead be its most primitive (early Elvish?) form.

This verb seems to have a sense similar to that of “to love, desire”. Perhap it is distinct from zîr- in that it has more to do with friendship than desire, so that the verb means “*to befriend” or “*to love (as a friend)”.

The 18th ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- “*Light-sword” (UT/222). If his Adûnaic and Quenya names have the same meaning, the second element of his name most likely means “sword”. The first element might mean “light”, as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/BAY’L), but the element bel- is attested elsewhere as a verbal element meaning “to love”. It is possible the two meanings coexisted, or that Tolkien changed the meaning of bel from “love” to “light”.

This name violates the original phonetic rules of Adûnaic, which said that the vowels and could only be long in Adûnaic (SD/423). See the discuss of for more information.

A noun attested only in its plural form bênî “servants” as an element in the term “Servants of God” (SD/341, 357). This noun resembles the Sindarin word “person”, especially in the Sindarin lenited form -ben. The Adûnaic noun may be related, having undergone phonetic development similar to that discussed for Ad. “word”, so that bên is ultimately derived from Primitive Elvish ✶ “person”, which could be its archaic meaning. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/BIN) that it is derived from a root *BIN, possibly related to Ed. “Vassal, Servant”.

A noun translated as “expression, saying, word” (SD/427). It is likely derived from the Primitive Adûnaic root √ “say” (SD/416). This word is very similar to Sindarin “word”, especially in the Sindarin lenited form beth. The ancient development of the Adûnaic word may have been similar to Sindarin, with Primitive Elvish root ᴹ√ > *√PET > ✶Ad. √BITH, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (/Adûnaic).
A root glossed “say” (SD/416), from which “expression, saying, word” is most likely derived. It may be related to the Primitive Elvish root √; see the entry on for further discussion.

A verbal form of Ad. “expression, saying, word” attested only as an as part of the noun “true-sayer” (SD/427); see that entry for further discussion of its phonetic development. As suggested by Thorsten Renk suggested (/24, 26), the verb stem is probably bith-, consistent with its primitive root ✶Ad. √. Since agental forms generally have a lengthened or fortified vowel, the verb stem bith- could have the fortified agental form -bêth.

An adjective glossed “heavy” (SD/247) or “very heavy” (VT24/12).

Conceptual Development: It appeared as buruda in early Adûnaic writings (SD/312).

A noun translated as “Earth” in the final version of the (SD/247). It may be related to S. “land”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/13).

Conceptual Development: In the , this noun appeared as (SD/311).

The noun for “Earth” in the first draft version of the Lament of Akallabêth (SD/311), later replaced by (SD/247). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/17) that it may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “soil, earth”.

A preposition translated as “under” (SD/247, 311) or “beneath” (VT24/12). It appeared in the usual suffixal position in the final version of the , but appeared before the noun it modified in the first draft version.
A noun translated as “gloom” derived from the root √ (SD/423). It is an example of how primitive , thereby producing diphthongs.
The root from which “gloom” is derived (SD/423), perhaps with a similar meaning.

A Primitive Adûnaic word glossed “gloom” (SD/423), the only attested example of a for a . Ordinarily such a form would not be possible, since final consonant clusters did not appear in Primitive Adûnaic (SD/418, 426). It is possible that such forms were valid in the case of medial semi-vowels [w] and [j], however, since , thereby preventing a cluster from forming.

A noun attested as the isolated word dolgu, described as “a word with the evil sense of ‘night’ or ‘dark’” (SD/306). It may be related to S. “night” and N. “obscure, hidden, dusky”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/13). It is similar to the word “black” appearing in the and the two may be variations of the same word, but most authors have suggested (/13-14, /Adûnaic, /DUL’G, /11, 24) that they are distinct words. In the phonetic rules in Lowdham’s Report from this period, a short o cannot appear in an Adûnaic (SD/423), so perhaps the proper form of this noun should be *dôlgu.

A verbal prefix in the first draft sentence azrē nai phurrusim akhās-ada (SD/311), expressing either the or verbal mood. It almost certainly related to Q. “maybe, may it be that” used for the expression of a wish, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/20). In later versions of the , this word was changed to .

A verb glossed “fell” in the (SD/247), but it is clear from context that its meaning is different from the ordinary verb for “to fall”: . Perhaps the sense of dubud- is “to fall under the influence of [shadow]” or “to fall under the cover of [shadow]”. Between the second draft and the final version version of the poem, the verb form changed from dubbudam ( tense) to dubdam (), in both cases with the plural verbal suffix .

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/23) that dubud- may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “loom, hang over oppressively”, which would fit well with the sense “to fall under the cover of”.

Conceptual Development: The draft form of the verb was udūbanim, which is difficult to analyze. It is missing a second d, so the draft verb may be a dū̆b- or perhaps a dūban-. Patrick Wynne and Carl Hostetter suggested (/35-36) that the initial u- may be a 3rd-person pronominal prefix, but I think it may instead be the vowel augment of a tense; see that entry for further discussion.

An adjective translated “black” (SD/247). It appears in its plural form dulgî “black” in the final version of the (SD/247) and in its singular form dulgu in the second draft of this text (SD/312). It may be related to S. “dark” and N. “obscure, hidden, dusky”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/14). It is likely related to or a variant of “black, dark”.
An adjective (or adverb?) translated as “far” (SD/247, SD/312).
A combination of “far” and the suffix (SD/247, 312), which could either mean “away” or be some kind of intensifier. See the entry for for further discussion.

gloss: far away now (is) the Land of Gift
notes:
The 13th phrase of the (SD/247). The first word “far away” is an adverb or emphatic adjective; see the entry for for further discussion. The second word “now” is an adverb. The last word “Land of Gift” is one of the names for Númenor. There is no subjective noun or a verb, so this phrase is a fragment rather than a full sentence.

The typescript version (and all earlier versions) had īdōn “now (is)” instead of īdō “now”. See the entry for for further discussion.

The first draft of the 13th phrase of the (SD/312). It differs from the final version mainly in its use of ēphalek “far away” for later and akallabēth instead of later ( appears instead in the last sentence of the final version). Like the final typescript version but unlike the final manuscript version, it uses īdōn “lo! now is” instead of īdō “now”. This is may be a combination of the adverb īdō “now” and the predicate suffix “is” used elsewhere in the draft version.

The 14th (and final) phrase of the (VT24/12). The first two words “far” and “far away” are repeated adjectives (or adverbs), the second with the added suffix -ak. This suffix either means “away” or is some kind of emphatic marker; see the entry for further discussion. The third word “now” is an adverb. The last word “The Downfallen” is the Adûnaic name for Númenor after its destruction. It is prefixed with the pronoun “she”, turning the name into a small sentence “She that hath fallen”.

The typescript version (and all earlier versions) had īdōn “now (is)” instead of īdō “now” (SD/247, 312). See the entry for for further discussion.

gloss: far far away is now the Land of Gift
notes: The first draft of the 14th (and final) phrase of the (SD/312). It differs from the final version mainly in its use of ēphalek “far away” for later and athanātē “Land of Gift” instead of later . In the final version of the Lament, another word for “Land of Gift” () appears in the second-to-last sentence instead. Like the final typescript version but unlike the final manuscript version, is uses īdōn “is now” instead of īdō “now”. This is likely a combination of the adverb īdō “now” and the predicate suffix “is” used elsewhere in the draft version.

The Adûnaic word for God (SD/432), the equivalent of Q. , though Tolkien had not yet coined that name. In the conceptual development of this name, Tolkien first invented it as an Adûnaic word (SD/312), only later adding it to Quenya. In this revised scenario, it is likely that the Adûnaic word was a loan word from Elvish. See Ad. for a similar development.
Another Adûnaic title for the Valar, translated “Servants of God” (SD/357). Since is “God”, the second element must be bênî “servants”, the plural of otherwise unattested “servant”

A title for the race of men as the children of “God” (SD/247). It is only attested in the plural Êruhîn (SD/311, 358) and subjective plural Êruhînim (SD/247-8) forms “Children of God”.

Conceptual Development: This name first appeared as Eruhil(di) (SD/341, 399), probably incorporating ᴹQ. “men”. In these early appearances Tolkien may have conceived of this as a Quenya word before introducing its Adûnaic form Êruhîn. In its early appearances the latter name sometimes had a short initial E: Eruhîn (SD/358), possibly another transitional form resembling later Sindarin . In still later writings, Tolkien coined a Quenya word Q. of the similar meaning, encompassing both Men and Elves.

gloss: [the Children of Eru] fell under shadow
notes:
The 2nd phrase of the (SD/247). Tolkien did not interpret the name Êruhînim in any version of the text, but elsewhere it is glossed “Children of God (Eru)” (SD/248). Tolkien’s gloss was “‽ fell ‽shadow under/beneath”, with the translation of the last word differing slightly in the typescript (SD/247) and manuscript (VT24/12). In ordinary English the phrase might be “the Children of Eru fell under shadow”.

The subject Êruhînim of the sentence is the plural form of #. The verb dubdam seems to be in the form of # “to fall”, glossed in past tense because it is in a narrative occurring in the past. The verb has the plural marker in agreement with the number of the subject. The word “under, beneath” is suffixed to the noun it modifies, as is usual of Adûnaic .

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence (SD/312) differs only in its use of the verb form dubbudam ( tense) instead of the final version’s form dubdam (). The first draft version used all the same words but differed in its grammar.

The first draft of the 2nd phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version only in grammar. The subject of the sentence seems to be a simple plural of #, not in the subjective case. The verb might be inflected with the 3rd-person singular masculine suffix u- “he”, but this contradicts the plurality of the subject. Another explanation is that the verb is in the tense and the initial u- is an augment vowel. Either way, it is difficult to explain why it has the verbal suffix -nim instead of the usual plural suffix .

The word “under” comes before the noun rather than as a suffix as is usual of later Adûnaic . The word it modifies seems to be the case of the word “shadow”, indicating that the objects of prepositions could be declined into various cases in the draft grammar.
One of the roots Tolkien used to illustrate various processes of Primitive Adûnaic word formation (SD/422-5). It also seems to be the basis of words related to stars, such as .

A collective-noun meaning “all the stars of the heavens”, as opposed to which was used for an individual star (SD/427). The element gimil appears in many names, including several later names in The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/15) that it may be related to the Elvish root √ “shine (white)”.

Andreas Moehn suggested (/KH-B-L) that if the later name means “Silver-fire”, its initial element gimil could instead mean “silver”, perhaps as a cognate of Dwarvish . If so, this alternate meaning could either be a homonym of gimil “stars”, or a new meaning for gimil in Tolkien’s later works.

Younger brother of Ar- (Q. Tar-) who was the 24th ruler of Númenor (S/269). His son Ar- usurped the throne to become the 25th (and final) ruler of Númenor. The first element of his name, means “stars”, but it is not clear what last element means.

A title of the goddess (Q. ) translated “Star-kindler” (SD/428), and therefore the Adûnaic equivalent of S. . The first element means “stars”, and the second is an for the verb “to kindle” (SD/427-8).

Second son of the 18th ruler of Númenor Ar- (Q. Tar- “*Light-sword”) and younger brother to the 19th ruler Ar- (UT/227). The first element means “stars”. The second element most likely means “sword” if his father’s Quenya and Adûnaic names have the same meaning.

Gimilzôr was the Adûnaic name of (SD/380) in the story “The Notion Club Papers” from the mid-1940s. Since the element means “stars”, this name is most likely a translation of the Sindarin name, which means “Star-foam”.

In later writings, Gimilzôr is the son of Ar- and the 23rd ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- (S/268). It is unclear whether this instance of Gimilzôr retains the same meaning as the earlier version of the name. It is possible that the later version has the same meaning as Telemnar (translated by most authors as “Silver-fire”), in which case Tolkien may also have revised the Adûnaic name of Elros (the word for “foam” was elsewhere given as Ad. roth). Alternately, it could be that the Adûnaic and Quenya names are unrelated, and Tar-Telemnar simply adopted the Adûnaic name of his illustrious ancestor.

Andreas Moehn suggested (/KH-B-L) that if Gimilzôr means “Silver-fire”, its initial element gimil “silver” could be a cognate of Dwarvish . Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that his Quenya name Telemnar contains adjective ᴹQ. “of silver”, and does not involve “fire” at all.

Conceptual Development: As a name for Eärendil, this name first appeared as (SD/363).

A draft Adûnaic name for “Star-foam”, later changed to (SD/363, 380). The final element may be the draft Adûnaic word for “star” mentioned by Christopher Tolkien on PM/372. If so, the first element might be a draft word meaning “foam”, but later words for foam such as Ad. are probably preferred.

Another name for Númenor translated “Starwards” (SD/378), the equivalent of Q. . Its first element is “stars” with the Adûnaic and its second element is the suffix -ad () “toward”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/15).
A noun translated “star” (SD/431) or “star (in the sky)” (SD/427), and fully declined on SD/431 as an example of a Strong II noun.

Christopher Tolkien mentions this as a noun meaning “star” from early and unpublished materials related to “The Notion Club Papers” stories (PM/372). It may be an element in the early Adûnaic name for . As Indilzar was replaced by , it is likely that azar was replaced by and , which are well attested in later writings.
An example phrase indicating how Adûnaic <a l="ad" v="numbers"/> follow plural nouns and are in a <a l="ad" v="genitive"/> relations with them: “seven of stars” (SD/427-8).
An example illustrating the difference between the singular noun “star” and the collective-noun “(all) stars” as used in the name “Star-kindler, kindler of all the stars” (SD/428).

A number translated as “seven”, appearing in the form hazad in the (SD/247), but in the form hazid in Lowdham’s Report (SD/427-8). Helge Fauskanger suggested (/Adûnaic) it may be related to the dwarvish word Khazâd “Dwarves”, who were divided into seven houses.

This element appears to be the object pronoun “me” in the phrase “don’t touch me” (SD/250). It is not clear whether it could also serve as a subject pronoun “I”. Thorsten Renk instead suggested (/18) that -hê may be a marker for the , and proposed the invented word Ad. !ni for “I, me”, a hypothetical cognate of Q. .

A Primitive Adûnaic form attested as i “she” (SD/435), but given the later feminine pronoun Ad. , the actual primitive pronoun must have been *HI [xi]. The suffix -i was also a common feature of Classical Adûnaic .

A pronominal prefix, the feminine singular pronoun “she” (SD/247). It appears in the pseudo-phrase hi-Akallabêth “She-that-hath-fallen” in the sentence and in the verb form hikalba “[she] fell” in the sentence “Númenor beloved fell (down)”. See the entry on for more discussion.
A noun translated as “ear” and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/430).

A Primitive Adûnaic form attested as u “he” (SD/435), but given the later Adûnaic pronoun Ad. or hu “he”, the actual primitive pronoun may have been *ƷU [ɣu], *ʔU or *HU [xu], as Tolkien indicated in a footnote (SD/433, note #7). The suffix -u was also a common feature of Classical Adûnaic .
An otherwise untranslatable name of a Númenórean commoner (UT/194).

A word translated “now” in the (SD/247). In the final manuscript version, this is the only form of the word, but in the final typescript version and in all earlier versions, it sometimes appears in the form îdôn.

Some authors have suggested this variation occurs when îdô appears before words beginning in a vowel or semi-vowel (/Adûnaic, /12), but this seems unlikely to me. Carl Hostetter, Patrick Wynne and Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/18, /16, , /DAW) that îdôn is a inflection of the word îdô, being used as a noun. The key evidence supporting this second theory is that where the form îdon appears, its gloss is always “now (is)” rather than simply “now”. As discussed elsewhere (SD/429), the inflection can function as the verb “to be”.

I tend to agree with this theory of Hostetter, Wynne and Moehn, but I think the actually development is somewhat more complex. In the first draft version of the Lament of Akallabêth, this form of the word appears twice as īdōn “lo! now is”. As noted by Mr. Moehn (), this version of the Lament used a predicate suffix “is” in several places: burodan “heavy-is”, rōkhī-nam “bent-are”. It seems likely that draft form īdōn “lo! now is” is another variation of this earlier syntax.

The draft predicate suffix differed from the later case in that it applied to the predicate of a clause instead of the subject. Compare these changes from the draft to final versions:

  • agannūlo burudan “death-shade heavy-is” >> agannâlô burôda “death-shadow [is] heavy”
  • batānī rōkhī-nam “ways bent-are” >> batîna lôkhî “ways (are) bent”

In both draft sentences, the subject is uninflected and the predicate has the predicate suffix -n/-nam. Conversely, in the later sentences the subject is inflected into the subjective case while the predicate is uninflected. This demonstrates the functional shift in the use of the predicate suffix -n in these drafts to the later use of the subjective inflection.

In both the second draft and final typescript versions of the Lament, the form îdôn was retained in all the sentences where it appeared in the first draft. This means that it could have been a remnant of this earlier syntax. The form îdôn could be reinterpreted as the sentence’s subject, but this is also problematic, since îdô is certainly neuter and its subjective form should be *îdôwa, not îdôn.

It is my belief that Tolkien eventually decided that the suffix -n could no longer be used in this context and removed it, switching to an uninflected îdô “now” everywhere in the text as is the case in the final manuscript version of the Lament. On the basis of this deduction, I also believe that the manuscript version was written after than the typescript version.

The 12th phrase of the (VT24/12). The first word is the adverb “now” and the second is the adjective “all”. Curiously, the adjective katha is not pluralized to agree with the noun as is the case with adjectives elsewhere in the text, including the pluralized lôkhî at the end of this very sentence.

The subject batîna “roads” is the plural form of the noun “road, path, way”. There is no verb, so the subjective form functions as the “to be” verb (SD/429). The final word lôkhî seems to be a pluralized adjective, perhaps #.

The typescipt version has kātha instead of katha, but is otherwise identical to the manuscript except some minor differences in translation (SD/247).

The first draft of the 12th phrase of the (SD/312). Although all of its word are similar to the final version, each has differences in grammar or spelling from the later versions of the text.

  • The first word īdō is the same as in the final version, but is glossed “lo! now” instead of simply “now”.
  • The adjective kathī “all” is the plural form of , not singular as it is in the final text, perhaps indicating a shift in the rules for adjective-noun agreement.
  • The subject batānī “ways” is the normal plural form of , not inflected to the case as it is in the final text.
  • The final word rōkhī-nam “(are) bent” has the plural adjective rōkhī instead of later form lōkhī. It also use the suffix -nam “are”, likely the plural of the predicate suffix “is”. This probably serves the same function as the inflection of the final version: to represent the “to be” verb “are”.
This noun is another singular variation of the collective-noun “(all) stars”, used for a “star-shaped figure” (SD/427) instead of an actual star which is .

The 22th prince of who fought at the battle of Pelennor fields in the War of the Ring (LotR/771). Tolkien said that “Imrahil is a Númenórean name” (LotR/1113), which seems to be true for the names of earlier princes as well (as discussed in the entry for ). It is not clear what this name means. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/16-17) that it may mean “Heir of Imra”, with the same initial element as and with -hil = “heir”. See the entry on for further discussion of the suffix -hil.

Conceptual Development: This name first appeared as Imrahil (WR/363), but Tolkien briefly changed it to Ildramir while he was concocting the name of , who at one point was similarly named Emrahil (SD/66). Once Tolkien settle on the name Arwen, the name of Imrahil was restored. In the drafts of the Lord of the Rings appendices, Tolkien initially listed Imrahil as a Lemberin (Nandorin) name (PM/36) before deciding it was Adûnaic.

The father of who became first prince of (UT/248). The name Imrazôr is Adûnaic in form and has the same initial element as , who was prince of Dol Amroth during the War of the Ring. It has the same last element as . It is not clear what this name means, however.

A draft Adûnaic phrase referring to (Elros) as the child of Azrabêl (Eärendil) which appears with and without the patronymic suffix (SD/365, 382). This phrase used an earlier form for the Adûnaic name of (instead of later ) and an earlier form Azrabêl of the Adûnaic name of his father (instead of later ). It also seems to include the suffix , although this could also be the inflection.
A noun meaning “flower” or more specifically “lily” (PE19/99). It appears as an element in Adûnaic names from the 1940s (Rôthinzil, SD/360) and later (Inziladûn, LotR/1035).

Son of Ar- and and the 24th ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- “The Farsighted” (LotR/1035). The meaning of his Adûnaic name is “Flower of the West” (UT/227), so he is an example of a Númenorean ruler whose Adûnaic and Quenya names had different meanings. The name Inziladûn was his given name and he adopted Palantir when he ascended the throne.

As pointed out by Andreas Moehn (/JIL), the ordering of the elements in this name are inconsistent with the rules outlined in Lowdham’s Report, which indicate that the adjectival element “West” should come before the noun “Flower” that it modifies (SD/428), so that the name properly should be *Adûninzil, similar to “Lord of the West”. The name as written would mean “West of the Flower”. Perhaps Tolkien relaxed or altered those rules in his later writings.

The wife of Ar- who was the 23rd ruler of Númenor (S/268). She was a secret Elf-friend and raised her son to be faithful to the Valar. Her name has the same initial element as her son: “flower”. The second element might be “word”.

An adjective glossed “straight” (SD/247), “right” (VT24/12) and “true” (SD/427), the last of these in the compound “true-sayer”. This final example is interesting, because the adjective izindi is declined into the case.

Conceptual Development: In its first appearance (SD/312), the form of this adjective was ezendi, an impossible form in the later phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, since Adûnaic only allowed the long vowel (SD/423).
A noun for “prophet”, more literally “true-sayer”, given by Tolkien as an example of the case combined with a verb stem in an (SD/427).

The primitive form of “sweetheart, beloved” (SD/424), probably derived from the root ✶Ad. √. The actual primitive word was more likely *izrai, produced via from the biconsonantal form *izri. Its plural form izray+yi is also attested.
A noun translated “sweetheart, beloved” and fully declined as an example of a weak II feminine-noun (SD/438).
A noun appearing only as an element in “city folk” (SD/435).
A compound noun translated “city folk” given as an example of an adjectival-genitive relationship between nouns (SD/435).

A word glossed “and so” in both the draft and final versions (SD/247, 311). This is the only known Adûnaic conjunction. Andreas Moehn suggested (/DAW, KA3) that the element -dô is some sort of modifying suffix, also seen in and , so that the conjugation “and” is simply ka. Thorsten Renk also used ka for simple “and” (/15).

The 1st phrase of the (SD/247). It changed little from its original draft, with only the verb unekkū becoming unakkha. Tolkien did not interpret the name Zigûrun in any version of the text, but it can be equated to Sauron from information given elsewhere (SD/250). Tolkien’s gloss was “and so ‽ humbled he-came”, which in more ordinary English might be “and so Sauron he came humbled”.

The subject Zigûrun of the sentence is the form of the name . The verb unakkha has the 3rd-person singular masculine inflection u- “he”. In the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, the subject would be emphasized with this syntax (SD/429), so the sense might be more like “and it was Sauron who came humbled”. It could be that the “so” of the English gloss is a representation of this emphasis, and that the initial word is simply the conjugation “and”.

The verb form nakkha is the tense of “to come”. Since the majority of the text seems to be in the , this use of the past tense would function as a pluperfect according to the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report (SD/439). If so, the sense would be more like “Sauron had come” rather than “Sauron came”. Finally, the position of the adjective “humbled” is difficult to explain, since Tolkien stated that “adjectives normally preceded nouns” (SD/428). Perhaps it follows because it is used as a predicate of the subjective subject Zigûrun (a construction discussed on SD/429), so that the literal interpretation of the full phrase would be “*and so Sauron [was] humbled, he had come [to Númenor]”. Alternately, zabathân could appear in this abnormal position because it is a (verbal adjective).

The first draft of the 1st phrase of the (SD/311), differing only from the the final version in its use of the verb (h)unekkū for later unakkha. In the draft, Tolkien changed the 3rd-person singular masculine suffix in this sentence from hu- to u- as he vacillated over the proper form of this inflection.
A Primitive Adûnaic root gloss “fall” (SD/416) appearing as an element in the name (PM/158) and also most likely the basis for the verb “to fall (down)”.

A verb translated “fall down” (SD/439). This verb has more conjugations than any other attested Adûnaic verb, and is therefore useful for studying the Adûnaic verb system. Excluding the first draft of the , it appears in four forms: ukallaba “[he] fell” (SD/429), hikallaba “she fell (down)” (SD/427), hikalba “she fell” (VT24/12) and yakalubim “lean over” (SD/251). Andreas Moehn suggested (, /KAL’B) the last of these could be a different verb kalub- “to lean”, but I think it is likelier to be a form of kalab-, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/26-27).

Various verbal prefixes and suffixes can be extracted by comparison to other forms: the pronominal prefixes u- “he”, hi- “she” and ya- “they (neuter)”, as well as the plural verb suffix . Removing these elements, we have three distinct forms: kallaba “fell”, kalba “fell” and kalubi “lean over”. These likely represent distinct verb tenses. The question is: which ones?

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/26-27) that kalubi is most likely the with the literal sense “*are falling over”, a conclusion with which most other authors agree (/Adûnaic, /14). Andreas Moehn agreed on this verb tense (, /KAL’B), but suggested that it is from the verb kalub- “to lean” instead.

The two remaining forms kalba and kallaba both have the gloss “fell”. This ambiguity is because the Adûnaic tense could used to describe the past in a narrative (SD/439). Most authors agree that these forms are the Adûnaic and tenses respectively, though Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested that kallaba is the instead (/27-28). See the entry on the Adûnaic tense for further discussion.

Finally, there is form appearing only in the draft versions of the Lament: akallabi “fell in ruin”. I believe this is an example of tense; see that entry for further discussion.
A noun translated “woman” (SD/434).
A verb translated “hold”, given by Tolkien as an example of a <a l="ad" v="biconsonantal-verb"/> (SD/439). There is unfortunately no information on how it might be conjugated.
An unglossed root (SD/415), likely the basis for the noun “horse” (SD/434).
A noun translated “horse”, given by Tolkien as an example of how can be altered into masculine and feminine forms using the suffixes and : karbî “mare” and karbû “stallion” (SD/434).

A word translated “all” in the (SD/288, VT24/12). This word appeared in the form kâtha in the final typescript version of the Lament (SD/247), but in all other instances appeared as katha. If the final typescript is later than the final manuscript, kâtha may be its final form, but I believe that the manuscript was later, and katha better matches its appearance as an element in “conqueror” (SD/429). This last example is interesting in that it is an example of an adjective declined into the case.

A noun translated “conqueror” (SD/429), apparently a compound whose first element seems to be the form of “all”. The final element is likely the agental suffix also attested in and . If so, the middle element is probably a verb, perhaps a triconsonantal verb *, though it could be a derived verb *phazgâ-.

A Primitive Adûnaic word glossed “crow” (SD/426). Tolkien gave two primitive forms of this word, khāw and khăw, which could just be variant forms of the same root *KHAW. A more intriguing possibility is that khāw is actually the form of khăw, since this would indicate that this subjective formation dates back to the primitive stages of the language. As evidence of this, the derived plural khāwī(m) (SD/426) does resemble the Classical Adûnaic subjective plural.

Contradicting this conjecture is the fact that khaw, as an animal name, should be declined as a common-noun, using the common subjective suffix . Elsewhere, though, Tolkien declined some animal names as if they were neuter nouns, for example narîka as the subjective plural of # (SD/251). Perhaps not all animals were common nouns, or perhaps Tolkien’s ideas for the subjective tense were not fully formed when these examples were written.

A verb appearing only as akhaini “lay” in the first draft of the Lament of Akallabêth (SD/312). In later versions of the Lament it was change to the verb “to go”, but since this replacement has a different sense, perhaps khay- remains valid.

This verb is only attested in the form akhaina “lay” and like all the draft verbs is difficult to analyze. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne analyze its initial element as the 3rd-singular pronominal suffix a- and its final element -ni as a past tense marker (/34, 37), also suggesting it may be derived from the Elvish root √ “lie (down)” (/10). This Elvish derivation seems likely to me, but I think the form of the verb may instead be the .

Thorsten Renk suggested (/35) the verb stem may instead be khain-. While he could be right about its use in the draft Adûnaic language, this doesn’t fit the later phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, which allow only long in Classical Adûnaic (SD/423).
A noun translated “spring” and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/430).

A noun translated “crow” (SD/426). Tolkien listed this noun in two forms, khâu and khô, both as examples of seemingly uniconsonantal nouns that prehistorically were biconsonantal (from prehistoric ✶khaw). Most authors have suggested these are simply variations on the same noun illustrating different paths of phonetic development (/18, /Adûnaic). Another interesting possibility is that khâu is an (archaic?) form of khô, produced from the usual a-fortification of primitive ✶khaw → ✶khāw, which would develop phonetically in Classical Adûnaic to khâu and khô. As support for this idea, the plural form of khâu is given as khāwī(m), which appears to include the subjective plural suffix .

This line of reasoning is quite speculative. Nevertheless, it is probably easier to use the form khô over khâu, since the inflections of khô would be more regular: plural khôi, dual *khôwat, objective *khôwu, etc.

An element meaning “lord” appearing only in the name “Lord of the West”, though a similar form appears in the earlier names “Lord” and “Lord of Darkness”. It isn’t clear whether this element is *akhôr or *khôr, but khôr resembles the Primitive Elvish root √ “rule, govern, possess”, to which it may be related.

This possible relationship has been suggested by various authors (/Adûnaic, /KHUR). Andreas Moehn rejected the relationship, pointing out that Primitive Elvish ✶khēru “lord” would have developed phonetically into Ad. **khîru (). However, khôr may be derived from some more ancient Avari loan word, which underwent different phonetic developments than those of the Eldarin languages, perhaps ✶kher- > khar > khaur > Ad. khôr.
A pronominal prefix, most likely the second person pronoun “you”, appearing in the verb kitabdahê “[you] touch me” in the sentence (SD/250). See the entry on for more discussion.
An unglossed root with a different meaning than (SD/415).

A noun appearing only in its plural form kulbî “roots”, corresponding to the collective-noun “roots, edible vegetables that are roots not fruits” (SD/431). As such, it most likely refers to root vegetables only, rather than other senses of the English word “root”.

One of the Primitive Adûnaic roots Tolkien used to illustrate the processes of Primitive Adûnaic word formation (SD/422-5). It also seems to be the root of words such as and “root (as a kind of plant)” (SD/431), perhaps an deliberate pun by Tolkien.

gloss: roots, edible vegetables that are roots not fruits
notes: A collective-noun meaning “all edible root vegetables”, as opposed to used for an individual root (SD/431).

A noun appearing only as an element in “city folk” (SD/435). It may be related to Q. “people”, as suggested by various authors (/18, /Adûnaic, /LAI). In at least one Avari dialect, this word was lai (WJ/410).

This text is the only substantial work in Adûnaic, appearing in Tolkien’s unfinished story “The Notion Club Papers” (SD/145-327). In the context of this story, a modern Englishmen named Lowdham retrieves the tale from visions of the ancient past, along with a Quenya translation of the same text. The text summarizes the tale of the fall of Númenor. Tolkien himself did not name the text, but it is sometimes referred to as the “Adûnaic Fragments” (SD/311, VT24/14). This entry uses the title “Lament of Akallabêth”, the Adûnaic equivalent of the common title of its Quenya version, the .

There are three known versions of the text:

  • A first draft (SD/311-12) written before the grammar of Adûnaic was fully developed, which uses the draft version of Adûnaic grammar.
  • A second draft (SD/312) using the final form of Adûnaic grammar, fairly close to the final version. The second draft has not been formally published, but it can be reconstructed from Christopher Tolkien’s notes on SD/312.
  • A final version which exists in nearly identical typescript (SD/247) and manuscript (VT24/12) forms, with somewhat different English translations. The full manuscript form originally appeared on the frontpiece of the British first edition of Sauron Defeated. It also appeared in the linguistic review of that book in (VT24/12).

Christopher Tolkien was uncertain which of the typescipt or manuscript was the true final revision of the text (SD/289). Andreas Moehn () and Aleš Bičan () both suggested that the typescipt is the later of the two, but I believe it is the manuscript, based on its cleaner glosses and the development of “now” in the sentences and (see the entries for and the draft predicate suffix for further details).
