Both texts are extremely close, however, and can be collectively called the “final version”.

The version given here is the final manuscript version, with spelling normalized to use the circumflex (â) for long vowels instead of the macron (ā). In the original version, English glosses appeared underneath words to indicate their literal meaning. The English translation given here is a combination of the manuscript and transcript translations, modified to use more natural English with some editorial additions in [brackets] where Tolkien omitted names and definite articles from his English translation. Original glosses and textual variations are discussed in the entries for individual phrases. The entire first draft is given its own entry below as a specimen of the draft version of the Adûnaic grammar.

Another analysis of this text can be found in “Lalaith’s Guide to Adûnaic Grammar” by Andreas Moehn (). A less formal analysis can be found in the “Verbs, Syntax, Hooray!” article (VT24/14-38) by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne, which analyzes much of text as part of their general discussion of Adûnaic grammar.
elements: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô

notes: The first draft of the (SD/311-2), presented in full here as a specimen of the draft Adûnaic grammar.

An adjective variously glossed as “bent” or “crooked”, attested only in its plural form lôkhî (SD/247, VT24/12). Andreas Moehn suggested (/LUKH) it may be related to the Elvish root √ “bend, loop”.

Conceptual Development: In its first appearance, this adjective had the plural form rōkhī, suggesting an earlier singular form *rôkhi (SD/312).

A noun translated “night” or more fully “fair night, a night of stars”, a late loan word from Q. (SD/414-5). According to Tolkien, it has a pleasant connotation similar to its Quenya equivalent: “it is a word of peace and beauty and has none of the associations of fear or groping that ‘dark’ has” (SD/306). Some unpleasant words for night and darkness are , and .

A prepositional suffix translated “with” (SD/247, 429).

Conceptual Development: At an earlier conceptual stage, it was the grammatical inflection used for the (SD/438).

A hypothetical verb from which the “wright, *builder” is derived, itself attested only as an element in the name “Shipwright”. It may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “use, handle”, as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/MAG).

A noun meaning “wright” attested only as an element in the name “Shipwright” (PM/151). It seems to be an of a verb ? “build” with the agental suffix . Therefore, its literal sense might be “*builder”.
The primitive form of “spirit” (SD/424). Its plural form manaw+yi is also attested.

A noun translated “spirit” and fully declined as an example of a Weak II noun (SD/438). It appeared with both a short a (SD/424) and long â (SD/438). Given its ending -ô, it might be a masculine-noun, but it seems unlikely that spirits would only be male. This entry assumes it is a common-noun instead. It is probably related to ᴹQ. “departed spirit” as suggested by various authors (/19, /Adûnaic, /MAN).
An unglossed word that it is apparently the masculine equivalent of “baby girl”, using the masculine suffix (SD/427).

An Adûnaic noun for “the heaven” or “sky”, cognate of Q. but not a direct loan word from Quenya (SD/241). It was borrowed from Primitive Elvish, probably from an Avari dialect, and therefore underwent different phonetic development (SD/414). In one place Tolkien changed it minil (SD/414), but the form minal appears in various compounds and is probably to be preferred.
A draft Adûnaic word for “the heavens”, later replaced by (SD/305).

A non- that contrasts with the name “Pillar of Heaven” (SD/429). Since the phrase is not objective, it must be a genitive relationship, who meaning according to Tolkien was something like “a pillar in the sky, or made of cloud”.

The name of a planet in Tolkien’s unfinished story “The Notion Club Papers”, translated “Poise in Heaven” (SD/200). Its language is not specified, but it is probably Adûnaic, since its first element is the Adûnaic word for “heaven”. If so, its second element must mean “poise”.

A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “heaven, sky” that Tolkien used as an example of an “early borrowing” from Primitive Elvish: the Primitive Elvish root √ became ✶Ad. √MINIL from whatever Avari language influenced Primitive Adûnaic (SD/414).

The Adûnaic name of the Pillar of Heaven (Q. ), the great and holy mountain at the center of Númenor (SD/249). The first element is the objective form of “the heavens”. The second element “pillar” is normally a noun, but in this case it behaves verbally with the sense “that which supports”, since the case requires a second verbal element (SD/429). Therefore, the literal translation of the name is “That Which Supports the Heavens”.

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name for this mountain was Menel-tūbil or (SD/305, SD/363).

A draft version of the Adûnaic name for the Pillar of Heaven, (SD/363). There are several variations, one of which, Meneltyūlā, might either be a Quenya word or from a draft version of Adûnaic that is closer to Quenya.
An Adûnaic noun for “little or baby girl” (SD/427, 437), fully declined on SD/437 as an example of a Weak I noun. It is also given as an example of a feminized noun form on SD/427.

A root glossed “small” that Tolkien wrote in its ✶Ad. √MIYI (SD/427). For consistency this entry has normalized it to the basic form of biconsonantal roots. Although glossed as “small”, all of its attested derivatives have to do with babies.
A noun attested only in its dual form miyât “(infant) twins” (SD/427). Its masculine and feminine equivalents are and .

The Adûnaic name of ; it seems to be a loan word from Q. “Mighty Arising” (or some Avari variant of it), but it is glossed “Lord of Darkness” (SD/358). If this is the meaning of the word, the final element could be related to “lord” appearing in the later name “Lord of the West”, or to the older rejected name “Lord”, also referring to Melkor. The initial element Mul- could perhaps be a distant variation on the Elvish root √ “dark”. Yet another possibility is that it was originally an ancient Elvish loan word (✶milikûr?) that shifted in form to resemble the meaning “Lord of Darkness”.

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic name for Morgoth, Mēlekō, was more clearly based on ᴹQ. , which was the Quenya name for Melkor in that stage of Tolkien’s writing.

A prepositional element only attested in the late (1968) word “hind-track”, referring to the wake behind a boat, so perhaps meaning “*behind” (PM/376). It appears only as a prefix, but in the earlier Adûnaic grammar of Lowdham’s Report (1946), Adûnaic are used as suffixes (SD/435).

An Adûnaic noun translated “hind-track”, referring to the wake behind a boat (PM/376). It appeared more than two decades (1968) after Tolkien’s Adûnaic Grammar in Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s (SD/413-440). This noun is inconsistent with the earlier grammar in two respects. First, the prepositional element nad- appears as a prefix, not as a suffix as did in the earlier grammar (SD/435). Second, it includes a short o, whereas in the earlier phonetic rules of Adûnaic, only a long is allowed (SD/423). See the entry on for further discussion.

An otherwise unexplained root that Tolkien used to illustrate the processes of Primitive Adûnaic word formation (SD/422-3). It may have no real meaning. Even if it were, certainly only a few of its derivatives could be real words in Classical Adûnaic.
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “come, approach” (SD/416), no doubt the basis for the verb “to come”.

A verb translated in the past tense as “came” (SD/247, 311), so probably meaning “to come”. Like , this is one of the few Adûnaic verbs attested in more than one conjugation. As such, it is useful in the study of Adûnaic verbs, in this case s as opposed to triconsonantal kalab-.

It is attested in two forms, unakkha “he-came” and yanākhim “are at hand”. The initial elements in these forms are the 3rd-sg masculine pronominal prefix u- and the 3rd-pl neuter pronominal prefix ya-, respectively, while the latter form has the plural verbal suffix . Removing these elements leaves the conjugated forms nakkha and nākhi, which are the and tenses according to the theories used here. If the second form is the continuative-present, its literal meaning may be “are coming”.

Conceptual Development: In the draft version of the Lament of Akallabêth, this verb stem was apparently nek-, with past forms hunekkū >> unekkū “he-came”, with Tolkien vacillating on the proper form of the 3rd-sg masculine pronominal prefix u-.

A noun attested only in the compound agannâlô “death-shadow [is]” (SD/247, VT24/12). The first element of the compound, “death”, as identified elsewhere (SD/426), so the remaining element must mean “shadow”. The compound is the subject of the sentence “death-shadow [is] heavy on us” and is therefore in the case. According the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, the only possibly normal form producing this subjective is nâlu: compare “moon” to its subjective form nîlô (SD/431).

Conceptual Development: In early writings, the compound was (non-subjective) agannūlo, so that the apparent draft form of this noun was nūlo. A similar form nūlu appears on SD/306, described only as “a word with the evil sense of ‘night’ or ‘dark’”. It could be a separate word or another variation of this word, with the development nūlo >> nūlu >> nālu. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/21) that the earlier forms may be related to ᴹQ. “dark, dusky, obscure”.

A noun attested only in the plural form Narīka “eagles” (SD/251). This formation is peculiar, because it seems to be a neuter subjective form, but the names of animals are generally , as pointed out by Andreas Moehn (/NAR’K). If it were declined as a common noun, the subjective plural should be *narkim: compare “Elf” whose subjective plural form is nimrim (SD/436). Perhaps when Narīka was written, Tolkien had not finished working out the Adûnaic gender and case system.
A noun translated “soldier” and fully declined as an example of a masculine Weak II noun (SD/438). Several authors have suggested (/20, /NERE) that it may be related to “man”.

gloss: The Eagles of the Lords of the West are at hand
notes:
An isolated Adûnaic sentence in “The Notion Club Papers” story (SD/251). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/26) that this same sentence is mentioned previously on SD/231 where Lowdham speaks in “an unknown tongue”, and then cries out in English “Behold the Eagles of the Lords of the West! They are coming over Nūmenōr!”. If so, this provides another translation of the phrase.

The first word, Narîka “Eagles” seems to be the plural of # “eagle”, but is unusual in that it is declined as if it were a neuter noun. The names of animals are generally (SD/426). Perhaps when this sentence was written, Tolkien had not yet fleshed out the Adûnaic rules.

Narîka is modified by the noun phrase ’nBâri “of the Lords”, which is a combination of the genitive prefix “of” (elided) and the plural of the noun “lord”. This is also unusual in that it uses the short i rather than the long î for the plural, another sign that this may be an early sentence (the Adûnaic often used a short i).

The phrase is further modified by ’nAdûn “of the West”, another instance of an elided genitive prefixed to the noun “west”.

The verb yanâkhim is glossed “are at hand”. Its initial element ya- is likely the third neuter person plural pronominal suffix “they” and it ends with the normal plural verb suffix . This leaves the verb form nâkhi, which seems to be an inflection of the verb “come”. A literal interpretation might be “*The Eagles of the Lords of the West are coming”, as supported by the second translation mentioned above, so that this is an example of the Adûnaic tense. This analysis of yanâkhim was suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/27).

A noun translated “soldier” and fully declined as an example of an (archaic) masculine Strong II noun (SD/437). The archaic form of this word is †naru which is a Strong II noun since it ends in a single short vowel. Its non-archaic form is narû, which is presumably declined as a Weak II noun; most masculine and feminine nouns became weak in Classical Adûnaic (SD/436). It may be related to the Primitive Elvish root √, as suggested by several authors (/20, /Adûnaic, /NERE).

A first person plural object pronoun “us” attested only in the prepositional phrase “on us” in the , developing though the various drafts as nēnum >> nēnu >> nēnud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify the element nê as the pronoun (/20, , /14), which seems likely since the prepositional element is probably -num/nu/nud related to Q. “under”. It is not clear whether this pronoun can also be used as a subject pronoun “we”, or if it must always be an object “us”.
The masculine personification of “the moon” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name for Q. .

A noun translated as “moon” and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/431). It appears with both a short and long final -u, but Tolkien indicated that the form with long û is actually the personified form “Man in the Moon” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name of . Tolkien also listed the “later forms Nil, Njūl” (SD/306), one of which may be the Westron word for “moon”, most likely Wes. . Andreas Moehn suggested (/NUL) that this noun may be related to nûlo/nûlu/nâlu, but given the evil connotations of these words (SD/306) and the different stem vowels, this seems unlikely to me.
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “shine” (SD/416), apparently the basis for “Elf”.

A noun translated “Elf” (WJ/419) and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/436). In one place, its plural Nimrî was translated “Shining Ones” (SD/358), which indicates was probably derived from the Primitive Adûnaic root √.

Conceptual Development: In its earliest appearances from the 1940s, this noun had the plural form Nimrî (SD/358, 388) as opposed to later plural Nimîr (SD/388, 436), which could indicate either an earlier singular form Nimri or a variant syntax for formation. The word also appears in Tolkien’s Quendi and Eldar essay from 1959-60 (WJ/386), indicating that this word survived in Tolkien’s later conception of Adûnaic.
The Adûnaic word for the Elvish language (SD/414), most likely a combination of the word “Elf” (evidently with the Adûnaic ) and a suffix meaning “language”, perhaps .

The Adûnaic name for Q. “Elf-friend”, almost certainly with the same meaning (SD/247). The first element is the form of “Elf” and the second element is an for “*to love” (SD/389).

Conceptual Development: The first Adûnaic version of this name, Nimruzân, shares the same suffix as the first Adûnaic version of his father’s Adûnaic name .

A noun meaning “Elf-friend”, attested only in the () plural form Nimruzîrim (PM/151). It is identical to the Adûnaic name of Q. , which had the same meaning.

Conceptual Development: An earlier name for the faithful Númenóreans was (SD/347).

An early name of the Númenóreans who remained faithful to the Valar, later called the “Elf-friends”: Ad. Nimruzîrim, Q. . It is not clear what language this word belongs to, but it may contain the word Adûnaic word for the Valar: .

A noun translated “girl” and fully declined as an example of a feminine Strong I noun (SD/430). It is also used as an example of feminine nouns that use the suffix -i in their inflection as opposed to the usual -u: nithli (SD/431). Though not explicitly stated, nithli is also an example of the variant objective-with-syncope syntax discussed on SD/435. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/21) it may be related to the Elvish root √ “young”.

A verb attested only as an in the names “Star-kindler” and “kindler of a (particular) star” (SD/428). Thorsten Renk suggested (/32) the base verb is nitir-, and this seems to me to be the likeliest possibility. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/NIT’Y) that the verb stem may be nit-, and that the -îr is some kind of feminine agental suffix.

A preposition attested only in the phrase “on us” in the , changing through the drafts as nēnum >> nēnu >> nēnud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify -nud as the prepositional element (/20, , /14), perhaps related to Q. “under”. If so, it may be a derivative of the Elvish roots √ “under” or √ “down”, with a semantic shift to the meaning “on”.

A noun translated “fool” and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/437-8). It was later written in the form nîph (SD/426), but since all the attested declensions are based on nûph, the entry here uses the earlier form.

The word nûph is a common-noun but it has some example inflections with masculine and feminine suffixes: nûphun (masculine subjective), nûphin (feminine subjective), nûphi (feminine objective). This seems to be another way that an individual’s gender be indicated (“male fool”, “female fool”) instead of using explicit masucline and feminine suffixes like or .

A noun translated “parent” (SD/434). It also appears in the dual form nuphrât “father and mother”, but this dual form is peculiar. As a weak II noun, the dual form ought to be *nuphârat, as for example “road” → batânat “pair of roads” (SD/431). Its dual form seems instead to undergo the Adûnaic (vowel loss), which happens nowhere else with a long vowel. There is no obvious explanation for this irregular formation.

A prepositional suffix translated “from” (SD/429). In a few places, the suffix appears with the v (pronounced ) between it and a preceding u-vowel (SD/247, 249). It is likely related to the Quenya genitive inflection Q. .

Conceptual Development: At an earlier conceptual stage, this suffix was a grammatical inflection, the (SD/438).

A prepositional element only attested in the late (1968) word “fore-cutting” (PM/376), referring to the wake before a boat, so perhaps meaning “*before”. It appears only as a suffix, but in the earlier Adûnaic grammar of Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s, Adûnaic are used as suffixes (SD/435). This preposition also differs from the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, which allow only long in Adûnaic words. If this preposition were used in the grammatical and phonetic context of Lowdham’s Report (Middle Adûnaic), it might be the suffix *-ôb. See the entry on for further discussion.

An Adûnaic word translated “fore-cutting”, referring to the wake before a boat (PM/376). It appeared more than two decades (1968) after Tolkien’s Adûnaic Grammar in Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s (SD/413-440). It is inconsistent with the earlier grammar in two respects. First, the prepositional element ob- appears as a prefix, not as a suffix as did in the earlier grammar (SD/435). Second, it includes a short o, whereas in the earlier phonetic rules of Adûnaic, only a long is allowed (SD/423). See the entry on for further discussion.
A noun translated “hand”, given as an example of an apparent Adûnaic uniconsonantal noun, which had a but lost one of its consonants from its ancient form ✶Ad. (SD/416, 426).
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “hand”, the basis for the noun of the same meaning (SD/416).
The Primitive Adûnaic form of the noun “hand” (SD/426).

A noun meaning “gold”, the only Adûnaic word defined in The Lord of the Rings (LotR/1114).

Conceptual Development: This noun also appears in “Lowdham’s Report on the Adunaic Language” from the 1940s (SD/426).

The son of who usurped the throne to become the 25th and final ruler of Númenor, translated “Golden” (LotR/1114, S/270). His Quenya name was Tar-. Since Calion appears to mean “*Son of Light”, Ar-Pharazôn is an example of a Númenórean ruler whose Adûnaic and Quenya names had different meanings.

The first element in his name is the noun “gold”. Since Pharazôn is glossed “Golden”, the second element may be an adjectival suffix. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHAR’Z) that the name means “*Golden One”, closer to its Quenya equivalent, and that the suffix -ôn is a masculine variant of the agental suffix . Either way, the name is also notable in that it does not undergo the Adûnaic when its suffix is added.

Conceptual Development: The name also appeared in “The Notion Club Papers” from the 1940s (SD/311), in some examples inflected into the case (SD/247, 428-9).

A hypothetical verbal element in the noun “conqueror” (SD/429), whose literally meaning might be “*all-ruler” (kathu-phazg-ân). Andreas Moehn suggested (/PHAZ) that it may be related to “prince” and have the meaning “to rule”, whereas Thorsten Renk suggested (/27) that it might mean “to conquer”.

A noun translated as “prince, king’s son”, given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a , the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns (SD/436-7). By the time of Classical Adûnaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead.

A verb translated “to-gush” or “flow” appearing in the (SD/247 SD/311), in later writings attested only in the form phursâ. This form superficially seems to be the of the triconsonantal verb phurus-. Its two draft forms phurusam > phurrusim further support the idea that the verb stem is phurus-. However, ordinarily aorist forms end in a short -a, so perhaps there is something unusual about this formation. It also lacks the usual plural verb suffix appearing in first-draft version of the Lament, which would ordinally be required to agree with the plural subject. Since phursâ appears with the or prefix du-, perhaps it is a special (infinitive?) form of the verb.

Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHUR) the verb stem may be phursâ- instead of phurus, so that it is a . This isn’t consistent with earlier forms, but it is possible that Tolkien changed his mind about the basic verb form.
A noun translated “breath” and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/431).

A noun translated “dog” and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/437). It is also used as an example of a common-noun that can be altered to masculine and feminine forms rabô “male dog” and rabê “bitch” (SD/434).

A verb appearing in the with the past-tense translations “broke” and “rent” (SD/247, VT24/12), so meaning “to break, rend”. In the final version of the Lament it appeared as yurahtam “they rent”. The initial element of this form is the 3rd persons masculine plural suffix yu- “they”, while its final element is the plural verbal suffix , both in agreement with the plural subject Bârîm “Lords”. This leaves the basic verb form rahta, which is the tense according to the theories used here.

In the previous (second draft) version of the Lament, the verb form was urahta with the 3rd persons masculine singular suffix u- “he”, and no plural suffix -m. This is consistent with the subject in this version, which was the singular Bârun “Lord”.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/22) that this verb may be related to Q. “to break” (MC/223). It could also be related to the contemporaneous ᴹQ. “to break asunder” (Ety/SKAT).

Conceptual Development: In the first draft of the Lament, the form was rakkhatū, indicating the earliest form of the verb may have had the verb stem rakhat- instead of later rahat-.

An element appearing in the name “Foam-flower”, attested in later writings (1968) as roth (PM/369, 376). This later form is incompatible with the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report from the 1940s, which allowed only long in Adûnaic words. If this word were used in the phonetic context of Lowdham’s Report (Middle Adûnaic), it should be rôth, and in these earlier texts, the Adûnaic name of Eärendi’s ship was Rôthinzil with a long ô (SD/360). Even in later writings, Tolkien lists róþ ([rōθ] = rôth) as one of its possible forms (PM/369). See the entry on for further discussion.

The Adûnaic name of Eärendil’s ship “Foam-flower”, of the same meaning (S/249). This name appears in earlier writings as Rôthinzil with a long ô (SD/360). Its later form is a violation of the phonetic rules laid out by Tolkien in Lowdham’s Report, which said that the vowels and could only be long in Adûnaic (SD/423). The later form could be an Anglicanized or a Westronized form (where a short could appear), or it could indicate that Tolkien changed his mind about Adûnaic phonetic rules. Some linguistic notes from the 1930s suggest Tolkien at one point considered making the name Quenya (P19/49).
A word glossed “shout” (SD/426). Andreas Moehn suggested (/RUKH) that it may be a verb rûkh- “to shout”, but it appears in a list of nouns, so I think it likelier that it is noun form.

This root, glossed “scar, score, furrow”, appeared as part of a discussion of the origin of the Sindarin word S. “foam” appearing in the name “Star-foam” (PM/368-371). Tolkien was uncertain whether this Sindarin word could coexist with its homophone S. “copper-coloured”, and investigated the possibility that Elros was instead derived from a Beorian word “foam”. According to Christopher Tolkien, his father was forced to abandon this line of reasoning when he remembered that the unrelated name S. also contained this element, forcing it to be of Sindarin rather than Beorian origin (SD/371).

Despite all this, the related Adûnaic word Ad. roth “foam” survived in The Silmarillion in the Adûnaic name “Foam-flower” of Earendil’s ship. Therefore, perhaps this root remains valid. According to Tolkien, this root originally had to do with ploughs and ploughing, and was later used for the white crest of waves by analogy with the churning dirt of a furrow (PM/376).

A noun translated “assent” (SD/247). The second element of this word is probably “word” as suggested by several authors (/22, /BITH). It isn’t clear what the first element means.

Conceptual Development: In the draft versions of the Lament of Akallabêth, the form of this word was sōbēth (SD/311).

This word is attested only in , whose Quenya name is (UT/223). The first element of the Quenya name seems to be “shore”, so the first element of his Adûnaic name probably has the same meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adûnaic, /SAK’L).

The son of Ar- and the 22nd ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- (UT/223). Tolkien didn’t translate either name, but his Quenya name seems to mean something like “*Shore-son” ( “shore” + “-son”) and his Adûnaic name may have a similar meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adûnaic, /SAK’L). If so, the initial element * would mean “shore” and the suffix would mean “-son”.

The interpretation of the second element is less certain than the first. For example, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that is Quenya name Falassion is actually a genitive plural meaning “of the Coasts” and does not involve “-son” at all. They suggested the final -thôr may instead mean “one” or “lord” (/23).
An otherwise unexplained root Tolkien gave to illustrate a pronunciation example. It may not be a real root.
A word Tolkien used to illustrate Adûnaic pronunciation without giving its meaning (SD/421).
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “understand” (SD/416), the basis for the verb “to understand” and the noun “wise man” (SD/421).

A verb attested only in the form usaphda “he understood”, an inflection with the 3rd person masculine pronominal prefix u- (SD/421). Archaically its aorist form underwent phonetic changes to become †saptha, but it was later reformed to be consistent with other inflections of the verb (such as the tense *sapphada).
The primitive form of “wise man, wizard”, derived from the root ✶Ad. √ (SD/421). Its final element may be a primitive form of the agental suffix .

A noun translated “wise man, wizard” given as an example of the phonetic development of primitive aspirates in contact with stops (SD/421). According to Tolkien, it was pronounced [safθān], indicating that the combination pth would be pronounced as a voiceless labial fricative [f] followed by a voiceless dental fricative [θ]. Given the phonetic rules of Adûnaic, most voiceless stops would be pronounced as fricatives before another fricative in Classical Adûnaic.

The Adûnaic number “two” (SD/428). It seems likely that it is related to Q. “two”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/22), though it is unclear how the initial s- might have developed in the Adûnaic. It may also be related to the Adûnaic dual suffix , as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/SAT).

A noun translated “trump” illustrating the development of Primitive Adûnaic palatals, or <a l="pad" v="c-series"/> (SD/419). Perhaps its meaning is the older sense of the English word: “trumpet”; it seems unlikely it would refer to a suit of cards .

A noun translated “mast” illustrating the development of Primitive Adûnaic palatals, or (SD/419). This example may also be related to the draft (?Adûnaic) name for the Pillar of Heaven Meneltyūlā, which contains a word much like the cognate of sulum: Q. .

A verb translated “touch”, attested only in the phrase bâ kitabdahê “Don’t touch me!” (SD/250). The initial element is perhaps the 2nd person pronoun “you”, and the final element is perhaps the object pronoun “me”. This leaves the middle element tabda “touch”, which looks like the tense of a triconsonantal verb tabad-. Most authors agree with this decomposition of the verb (/TAB’D, /18, /Adûnaic), though Thorsten Renk suggested (/18) the final element is a marker of the imperative.

An adverb glossed as both “once” and “then” (SD/247, VT24/12). Several authors have suggested (/23, /TA3) that the final element may be “now”. Andreas Moehn suggested (/TA3) the initial element tâ is a marker that puts it into the past: îdô = “now”, tâ-îdô = “previous time” = “then”. It seems likelier to me that the prefix is related to the Eldarin demonstrative root √ “that, there, then”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/23): tâ-îdô = “that time” = “then”.

Conceptual Development: In the second draft of the , this word was ēluk (SD/312).
A noun translated “smith” and fully declined as an example of a masculine Strong I noun (SD/436). It may be related to the Eldarin root √ “construct”, as suggested by several authors (/23, /TAM).

The Adûnaic word for “pillar” (SD/241). Tolkien explained that this word is perceived as having a verbal function: “that which supports” (SD/429). As such, it can be used with an objective form in the name “That Which Supports the Heavens”.

Conceptual Development: In earlier drafts of “The Notion Club Papers” stories, this word appeared (SD/363), tūbil (SD/305) and (Quenya?) tyūlā (SD/346).
A draft version of “pillar” (SD/363), also appearing as tūbil (SD/305) and tyūlā (SD/346), the latter perhaps a variant of Q. “mast”.
A noun translated “land” (SD/435) appearing in the Adûnaic names for the Blessed Realm: and . Its Primitive Adûnaic form was also ✶, though its primitive was glossed “realm" (SD/420).

The primitive form of “land”, written in allcaps as THĀNI (SD/420). Usually Tolkien used capitalization for primitive roots, but in this case it is more like to be a form derived from an unattested Primitive Adûnaic root *√THAN.

A phrase demonstrating the use of the genitive prefix , elided to ’n in this case (SD/435). Earlier in the same discussion, Tolkien gave the non-elided (but less common) variant: thâni anAmân. It may be contrasted with the genitive compound in which the adjective element appears first.

A well-attested pronominal prefix, the masculine singular pronoun “he” (SD/433). See the entry on for more discussion. Tolkien said that it had another variant hu- (SD/433), but this variant was only appears in the early and rejected hunekkū, which was changed to unekkū (see ). Tolkien further indicated that the form u- primitively had an initial consonant [ɣ] or [ʔ] that was lost (SD/433).

A noun translated “shadow” (SD/247), also described as “a word with the evil sense of ‘night’ or ‘dark’” (SD/306). It appears in the preprositional phrase ugru-dalad “under shadow” (SD/247) and in the form ugrus “‽horror‽shadow” (SD/311).
A verb translated “overshadow”, given as an example of a (SD/439). It appears to contain the element “shadow”, so perhaps the final element is a causative verbal suffix.
An otherwise untranslatable name of a Númenórean commoner (UT/195).
The feminine personification of “the sun” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name for Q. .

A noun translated “sun” (SD/306, 428). This word appears in the forms ûrê, ûri and ûrî, but Tolkien declared that the form with long î is actually the personified form “Lady of the Sun” (SD/426), perhaps the Adûnaic name of Q. . The form ûrê only appears once (SD/426), so ûri is probably to be preferred as the ordinary word for Sun, especially since it is a neuter noun, which ordinarily cannot end in a long -ê (SD/427). Tolkien lists the “later forms Uir, Ŷr” (SD/306), one of which may be the Westron word for “sun”, most likely Wes. . As suggested by several authors (/24, /UR), ûri is probably derived from the Elvish root ᴹ√.

An isolated Adûnaic sentence in “The Notion Club Papers” story (SD/251). The subject urîd seems to be the normal plural of “mountain”. According to the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, this word is not required to be in the subjective because the verb has the pronominal prefix ya-, most likely the neuter form of “they”. The verb ends with the usual verbal plural suffix , leaving the verb form kalubi. It seems to be an inflection of the verb “to fall”, perhaps the form. If so, a more literal translation of the sentence would be “*the mountains are falling”.

This analysis of yakalubim was suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/27).
A phrase demonstrating a dual compound with two different elements. It contains the related pair “sun” and “moon (SD/428).
An example of a dual phrase with two different words. The first word of the pair is declined as a dual. It contains the related pair “sun” and “moon” (SD/428).

A noun attested only in its plural form urîd “mountains” (SD/251). Several authors have suggested it is related to S. “mountain”, either borrowed directly or derived from the same Elvish root ᴹ√ (/24, /ÓROT).
A noun translated “bear” (SD/426), also given by Tolkien as an example of how can be altered into masculine and feminine forms using the suffixes and : urgī “female bear, she-bear” (SD/435).

A noun translated “goblin, orc” and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/436). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/24) this form of the word may be a derivative of the contemporaneous Elvish root ᴹ√. In later writings it appeared as Ad. urku/urkhu (WJ/390), a derivative of the Elvish root √ “terrible shapes”. This entry retains the form uruk because of its many attested inflections.

A pronominal prefix, most likely the neuter/common plural pronoun “they”. It appears in the verb yanâkhim “[they] are at hand” in the sentence and in the verb yakalubim “[they] lean over” in the sentence (SD/251), both sentences having plural subjects. See the entry on for more discussion.

A verb appearing in the in the form ayadda “(it) went” (SD/247, VT24/12). Its initial element is the 3rd persons neuter plural suffix a- “it”. This leaves the basic verb form yadda, which is the tense according to the theories used here.

Conceptual Development: It appeared in the form yadda in the first draft version of the Lament, and this form was also briefly considered as a replacement for unakkha “he-came” in the first sentence of the Lament (SD/312).

The likely primitive form of the Classical Adûnaic plural inflection (SD/429), appearing in a few examples of primitive plurals in the form -yi: manaw+yi, izray+yi (SD/424). Tolkien gave no indication of whether the primitive inflection was also used as an infix, as was the case for Classical Adûnaic plurals of strong-nouns.
A hypothetical feminine plural pronoun “they”, assuming it follows the same pattern as masculine and neuter , as suggested by several authors (/Adûnaic, /14, ).

Ar-Zimrahil after he invented the Adûnaic language (SD/373). The suffix -hil in this version of the name might be a feminine form of the patronymic . In later material appearing in the published version of The Silmarillion, her Adûnaic name was changed to Zimraphel. The son of Ar- and the 21st ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- “*Many-jewels” (UT/222). The first element “jewel” of his Adûnaic name seems to have the same meaning as the last element -mir of his Quenya name. The first element ᴹQ. of his Quenya name means a “large number”, and this might be the meaning of the last element -thôn of his Adûnaic name, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/23).

Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/ZIM’R) that the final element may be the same as the final element of and that the entire name is an of an unattested verb *zimrathâ- “gather jewels”. A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “love, desire”, the basis for the verbal element of similar meaning and the noun “yearning” (SD/423). It is likely also the basis for the noun “sweetheart, beloved” (SD/424).

An Adûnaic verb appearing as an element in various compounds as -zîr or zîr- (SD/389, 423). The verb was not translated, but its primitive root form is glossed “love, desire”, so this verb probably has a similar meaning.

Several authors have suggested (/ZIR, /20) that the verb stem is zir- with a short vowel. However, the vowel is long in the participle form “beloved”, and there are tentative examples where a verb with a short vowel would retain that short vowel in the agental/participle form: “*builder”. I therefore think that the verb stem is likelier to be zîr-.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/25) that it may be related to the Middle-Period Elvish root ᴹ√.

An adjective translated “(the) beloved” (SD/247), apparently formed from the verb “to love, desire” with the participle suffix . Its placement in the sentence “Númenor beloved fell (down)” is unusual, since according to Tolkien adjectives normally precede the nouns they modify (SD/428). It is possible that the adjective here is being used as a noun “the beloved”, an idea supported by the translation of this sentence in the final manuscript: “Anadune the beloved she fell” (VT24/12). See the entry for the Adûnaic for further discussion.

An element in the names and . Imrazôr is difficult to translate, but Gimilzôr is equated to two different Quenya names at different periods of Tolkien’s writing: “Star-foam” in the unfinished “Notion Club Papers” story from 1946 (SD/380), and in the list of Adûnaic kings in The Lord of the Rings (LotR/1035). The name Telemnar is unglossed, but a likely translation would be “*Silver-fire”. Assuming the element zôr has the same meaning as its Quenya equivalents, could mean either “foam” or “fire”. There is a different Adûnaic word for foam: or roth in “Foam-flower”, so perhaps “fire” is a more useful interpretation, albeit quite speculative.

A noun translated “nurse” and fully declined as an example of a feminine Weak II noun (SD/438). It has two attested objective forms, an archaic form †zôrîyu using the ordinary objective inflection and non-archaic form zôrî, no doubt using the objective inflection -i- often used in feminine nouns (SD/432): zôrî + -i = zôrî.
A Primitive Adûnaic root glossed “one, alone” (SD/432), likely the basis for “God” (the One) and probably related to the Primitive Elvish root √ of the same meaning.

A noun that, together with its variant dang, was glossed “sound” (Ety/DING). Given that its root form ᴹ√ was said to be onomatopoeic, it was probably a word for a particular kind of sound, perhaps like English “twang”, which is a gloss of several derivatives of the similar root ᴹ√.

An Ilkorin noun for “head” attested only as an element in the name “Wet Head” (Ety/MIZD, NDOL). It might also appear in , assuming that name is Ilkorin. Assuming it functions similarly to its Noldorin equivalent N. , it can probably also be used to refer to a hill.
A noun glossed “flat, lowlying vale” (Ety/DAL). Helge Fauskanger pointed out that the gloss is ambiguous, and it may be that this word can also be used as an adjective “flat” (AL-Ilkorin/dôl).

A Doriathrin word for “back” explicitly marked as a noun (Ety/NDAN). Its primitive form might have been *✶ndān, so that the primitive long [ā] became [ō] and the initial nasal [n] was lost before the stop (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/dôn).
A Doriathrin noun for “land” (EtyAC/NDOR) apparently from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/NDOR). If its primitive form indeed had a short [o], then this word may be an example of how in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun meaning “oak” derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶dóron[o] (Ety/DÓRON). The accent mark in the root indicated that the first syllable was stressed, thereby preventing the initial [dor-] from becoming [dr-]. The second [o] was lost, however, due to the Ilkorin syncope.

A Doriathrin noun meaning “wolf” derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/DARÁK), probably from older *✶darākă. The accent mark in the root ᴹ√DARÁK indicated that the first syllable was unstressed, so that the initial [dar-] became [dr-]. Thereafter the long [ā], became [ō] and the voiceless stop [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel.
A noun meaning “river”, simply an elaboration of its root ᴹ√ (Ety/DUI).
A noun meaning “water, river”, simply an elaboration of its root ᴹ√ (Ety/DUI).
A noun for “twilight” developed from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/DOMO), where the long .

A Doriathrin adjective meaning “black” (Ety/DUN). Its Noldorin and Danian cognates imply development from a primitive form *✶dunnā. Since the primitive form ended in [a], the Ilkorin a-affection would ordinarily have produced **donn. However, it seems that a-affection was prevented or reversed before [nn], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/dunn).

A Doriathrin noun for “sorcery” (Ety/ÑGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots ᴹ√ and ᴹ√. If it were derived from such a primitive form, it would imply that in its phonological history the [o] because [u] in both syllables. This does not seem to be a general rule in Ilkorin, however: compare Ilk. and . A simpler explanation would be that it was a loan word from Noldorin: N. seen in a marginal note (EtyAC/ÑGOL).

Conceptual Development: There is a rejected form dûghol in this entry of The Etymologies that may represent Tolkien’s first attempt to formulate a native Ilkorin word for “sorcery” (EtyAC/ÑGOL). Similar forms appear among the precursors to S. in Lord of the Rings drafts from the 1940s: Dol Dúgol or (TI/178; WR/122). The entry also has a deleted variant form of gûl of Ilk. , so it may be Tolkien originally envisioned a different phonological history of [o] in Ilkorin allowing the production of words like durgul. Perhaps he added the Noldorin form durgul in the margin because he abandoned [o] > [u] in Ilkorin.
The Ilkorin name of ᴹQ. , developed from the same primitive form ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/EZDĒ).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “star”, a simple derivative of the root ᴹ√ (Ety/EL).

A rejected Doriathrin word for “Elf”, a derivation of the root ᴹ√ and a direct cognate of ᴹQ. , also appearing in its plural form Eldin (Ety/ELED). It was replaced by Ilk. derived from the inverted form of the root: ᴹ✶edel[a].
The Ilkorin word for “one” attested only in the name or Ermab(r)in “One-handed” (Ety/MAP).
A noun meaning “seed, germ” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/ERÉD). The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/erdh).

A noun meaning “sedge” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ESEK), probably from a primitive form *✶eseke. The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/esg).

A rejected noun meaning “rustle, noise of leaves” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/EZGE). Its (rejected) Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶eseke, despite the root form. If so, middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the .
A noun for “wound” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/SKAR). Apparently the initial [sk-] became syllabic [ṣk-], which then became [esk-]. Afterwards the .

A noun for “reed-bed”, apparently an elaboration of Ilk. “reed” (Ety/ESEK). In a hastily written entry in The Etymologies, a similar form esgar was glossed “shore” as a derivative of the root ᴹ√, but with no language specified (EtyAC/SKAR²). If it was Ilkorin, it probably underwent the same development as “wound”. Both these words appeared to have been coined to explain the name of the town from the Hobbit.

A noun derived from the root ᴹ√SPÁLAS and glossed “foaming (?fall)”; the second word in the gloss is unclear (Ety/PHAL). It was marked as Ilkorin (EtyAC/PHAL). Apparently the initial [sp-] became syllabic [ṣp-] and then became [esp-].

A Doriathrin noun meaning “fence” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GAT(H)), most likely from a primitive form *✶gat-. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gad), its gloss is a bit peculiar, given that the other derivatives of its root same to have meanings associated with caves. As Mr. Fauskanger suggested, this may represent a transition in Tolkien’s thinking on the meaning of the associated name : “Land of the Cave” (Ety/GAT(H)) >> “Land of the Fence” (WJ/370).

A Doriathrin (and Falathrin) noun for “beech (tree)”, a combination of “tree” and “(beech) mast” (Ety/GALAD, BERÉTH). The second element originally meant “beech”, but later meant “mast”; this original meaning seems to be preserved in this compound.

A Doriathrin noun for “tree” derived from the root ᴹ√GÁLAD (Ety/GALAD), probably from a primitive form *✶galadā with the second a lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope. Note that the first element [gal-] did not reduce to [gl-] because the initial syllable was stressed in the primitive word.

A noun meaning “harp” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÑGAN), probably from a primitive form *✶ngandellē based on its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. . Its plural form genglin is a good representation of the rules for in Ilkorin: the suffix , the syncope of the final vowel and mutation of other vowels. It is also an example of how primitive [nd] sometimes became [ŋg] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gangel).

A Doriathrin word (noun and adjective?) for a “male” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ƷAN).

Possible Etymology: Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶ʒanū [ɣanū], but ordinarily a primitive final vowel was lost in Ilkorin. Helge Fauskanger suggested that this Ilkorin word was instead derived for adjective form *✶ʒanwā [ɣanwā], which would have produced final -u after the loss of the [-ā] because final [w] became [u]. This derivation is indicated in the Phonetic Developments given below.

An alternate possibility, though, is that [u] was an exception to the rule that final vowels were lost in Ilkorin. The Noldorin development ᴹ√ƷAN > ON. > N. hints at a similar process. This uncertainly in its etymology makes it difficult to determine the part of speech (noun and/or adjective) that this word belongs to.

A Doriathrin noun for “wolf” derived from the root ᴹ√ÑGAR(A)M (Ety/ÑGARAM), probably from a primitive form *✶ŋgaramō given its Quenya and Noldorin cognates ᴹQ. and N. (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/garm). If so, the second a was lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope, and the the initial [ŋg-] simplified to [g-]. The initial syllable of the primitive form was probably stressed, since the initial [ŋgar-] did not simplify to [ŋgr-].

Conceptual Development: An earlier version of this entry had the root ᴹ√ƷARAM, but this produced the same form Dor. garm in Doriathrin [Ilkorin] since initial [ɣ] became [g].

A Doriathrin noun for “lord” derived from the root ᴹ√ or possibly ᴹ√GAR (Ety/ƷAR), perhaps from a primitive form *✶ɣarān-. If so, the initial [ɣ] became [g], while the long [ā] became [ō] and then shortened to [o] in the final syllable of a polysyllable.

Conceptual Development: An earlier version of this entry had Dor. garan, which likely had a short [a] in the second syllable which was preserved. Since it did not undergo the Ilkorin Syncope, the primitive form likely either had no final vowel or ended in a short [a], so the second [a] was in the final syllable, which seems to have prevented the syncope; this theory is supported by its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. .

An adjective meaning “bright” derived from the root ᴹ√, the basis of the river name (Ety/GYEL). There isn’t enough information to deduce its primitive form, but Helge Fauskanger suggested *✶galjānā (AL-Ilkorin/gelion), which seems reasonably plausible.
A Doriathrin noun for “sky” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ƷEL), probably from a primitive form *✶ʒellē [ɣellē] based on its cognates. It is a clear example of how initial [ɣ] became [g] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning “(pale) blue” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ƷEL), probably from a primitive form *✶ʒelwā [ɣelwā] based on its cognates. If so, the initial [ɣ] became [g], the primitive final [a] vanished, after which the final [w] became [u]. These developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gelu).
A noun meaning “dirtiness, filth” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/WAƷ). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gôd).

A verb meaning “to soil, stain” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/WAƷ). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments similar to those of related “dirtiness, filth”, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/góda-).

A (rejected?) Doriathrin noun for “light” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ appearing in The Etymologies (Ety/KAL, EtyAC/KAL). According to Christopher Tolkien’s notes, it was part of a rejected etymology for the name , but it isn’t clear whether this noun was rejected or if it was just the etymology. Its long primitive vowel [ā] became [ō] as was the norm in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin name for the Silmarils, a combination of the genitive form of “Noldo” and “jewel” (Ety/MIR, ÑGOLOD), hence: “*Noldo-jewel”. It also appeared in the variant form Goldomir, which may hint at the primitive form of the .

An adjective meaning “soiled, dirty” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ [waɣrā] (Ety/WAƷ). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gôr).

A noun glossed “shade” (shadow) derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/WATH). It is a clear example of how in Ilkorin, and it appears in several names: “(Woman of) Secret Shadow” and (unglossed but presumably “*Mountains of Shadow”).
A noun meaning “wind” derived from the root ᴹ√WAW(A) (Ety/WĀ). Here the , and after the final vowel vanished, the final [w] became [u].
A noun meaning “bond” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/WED). Here the , and the [d] spirantalized to [ð].

A noun for “air” or “the lower air”, derived from the same primitive form ᴹ✶ as its Quenya equivalent ᴹQ. Wilwa (Ety/WIL). Here the . Furthermore, after the final [a] was lost, the final [w] became [u] and then became [o], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwelo).

Conceptual Development: In the Addenda and Corrigenda to The Etymologies, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated the Tolkien revised this form to gwelm at the same time as he change its primitive to ᴹ✶wilmā and the Quenya form to ᴹQ. Wilma (EtyAC/WIL). This entry keeps the earlier Ilkorin form gwelo because Tolkien never revised ᴹQ. Wilwa in the narratives of this period.
A noun for “girl” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/WEN). Here the .
A noun for “greenness” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GWEN).

An adjective for “green” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. wenya suggests its primitive form was *✶gwenyā [gwenjā]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwene).

A noun for “butterfly” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. wilwarind- suggests its primitive form was *✶wilwarinde. If so, it is an example of how [nd] sometimes became [ŋg] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gwilwering).
An adjective for “pale blue” derived from the root ᴹ√GWINDI, rejected along with its root (EtyAC/GWINDI).

A noun for “evening” derived from primitive ᴹ✶winyā [winjā], but it was rejected along with its root ᴹ√WIN (Ety/WIN). It is the clearest example of the Ilkorin phonetic development whereby final [j] became [i] and then became [e], since Tolkien indicated the intermediate forms before rejecting the word.
A noun for “spindrift, flying spray” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/WIG). Here the .

A Doriathrin adjective for “grey” written heðu in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶ [kʰitʰwa] (Ety/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. The [i] became [e] before the final [a].
  2. Both the : [kʰ-] > [x-] and [-tʰ-] > [-θ-].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [-θ-] voiced to [-ð-] (“dh”).
  3. The primitive final [a] was lost.
  4. Afterwards, the resulting final [w] became [u].

In most other Doriathrin words, a final [u] from [w] further developed into [o]; it is unclear why this change did not occur here.
A noun glossed “captain” derived from the root ᴹ√ “command” (EtyAC/KHES). The language of this word is unclear; Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated it might be ?Bel. for Beleriandic = Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun for “fog” written hiðum in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form ᴹ✶ [kʰitʰme] (Ety/KHIS, EtyAC/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. Both the : [kʰ-] > [x-] and [-tʰ-] > [-θ-].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [-θ-] voiced to [-ð-] (“dh”).
  2. The primitive final [e] was lost.
  3. Afterwards, the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [-um].
A Doriathrin noun for “lady” attested only as an element in the name (Ety/NEL). It probably had essentially the same derivation as its Noldorin cognate N. (Ety/KHER).

A preposition “from, away” marked as both Ilkorin (Ety/ƷŌ̆; PE21/60) and Doriathrin (EtyAC/ƷŌ̆). It developed from primitive ᴹ✶ʒō̆ (Ety/WŌ), with the initial [ɣ] becoming [g]. It was also used as patronymic, as in go-Thingol “*child of Thingol” (Ety/ƷŌ̆).

Conceptual Development: This preposition may be a restoration of the Gnomish patronymic G. . In Tolkien’s later writings, Common Eldarin: Noun Structure (EVS2) from around 1950 mentioned a similar Beleriandic preposition ho “from” derived from ✶ʒō̆ which influenced a patronymic hon based on {✶jond- >>} ✶ʒond- “son”. This late appearance was shortly before he abandoned Ilkorin/Beleriandic entirely.
A word for “a blow with an axe” in Early Noldorin Word-lists of the 1920s derived from primitive ᴱ✶skantá (PE13/147).
The Doriathrin word for the “Moon” developed from the primitive name ᴹ✶ (Ety/I²), though it is unclear how the [st] developed. Perhap it was of the same origin as “silver light, starlight” (Ety/SIL).

A Doriathrin noun for “silver light, starlight”, also given as istel, which developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/SIL). Tolkien said that it was probably originally a (ancient?) Quenya word learned from Melian. This apparently this means its development was unusual. Along with the identical “Moon”, it is the only Ilkorin noun with a medial [st]. Helge Fauskanger suggested it must have developed by a strengthening of [s] to [st]. It may also be another example of a development from syllabic [ṣ], though elsewhere .

A rejected Doriathrin noun for “babe” developed from the root ᴹ√ (EtyAC/LAP). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form of *✶lapsē, but elsewhere a medial [ps] became [ss] in Ilkorin, as with < ᴹ✶.

An adjective meaning “fresh, lively” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/LÁYAK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/laig). This allowed it to blend with the derivative of ᴹ✶ and assume the additional meanings “keen, sharp” (Ety/LAIK).

A noun meaning “elm-tree” developed from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÁLAM). An identical form appeared elsewhere in The Etymologies with its language marked “D”, perhaps for Doriathrin (Ety/LÁLAM). This word is unusual in that its final [m] did not become syllabic after a consonant, although it did for other similar words such as .

gloss: licking up (food or drink), gluttonous eating

notes: A Doriathrin noun for “gold” developed from primitive ᴹ✶, properly golden light rather than the metal (Ety/LÁWAR).

An adjective meaning “tuneful, sweet” developed from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIND, EtyAC/LIND). It is an example of how the usual Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [nd], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/lind). This word may also have had the sense “*singing” in the word “nightingale = *night singing”, from primitive ᴹ✶.

A noun for “pool” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/LIN¹). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests its primitive form was *✶linyā [linjā]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/line).

A Doriathrin noun for “fish” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is the clearest example of how , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/líw). @@@ same development in ᴱN hiw PE13/147

Conceptual Development: This word first appeared as rejected ling (EtyAC/LIW), probably reflecting Tolkien’s uncertainty on the development of [-ŋgw-] in Ilkorin.
Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of “echoing” and “land”.
Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of “echoing” and the plural of “mountain”.

An adjective meaning “empty” attested only as an element in the Ilkorin name (Ety/MAP). As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, it might be a combination of Dor. and the adjective suffix , but if so it is unclear where the medial g came from (AL-Ilkorin/Mablosgen). Alternately, perhaps losgen is the general Ilkorin adjective for “empty” and lost is a variant used only in the Doriathrin dialect.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning “empty” attested only as an element in the name Dor. (Ety/KAB). Its Quenya cognate suggests a primitive form *✶lustā, with the [o] developing from Ilkorin a-affection. It might be a Doriathrin-only variant of more general Ilkorin “empty”.

A Doriathrin adjective for “pale” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, a revision of the form luin that appeared in The Etymologies as published in The Lost Road (Ety/LUG², EtyAC/LUG²). The revision of [ui] >> [ū] probably reflects Tolkien’s vacillation on how primitive in Ilkorin. The earlier form of this word might an element in the name “Werewolf” (LR/134), which in earlier writings was glossed “Werewolf Pale” (LB/205). The early Noldorin word ᴱN. “pale” might be a precursor to it (PE13/149).

A Doriathrin adjective for “heavy” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LUG¹). It is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [ŋg], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/lung).

An unglossed Doriathrin word derived from the root ᴹ√ “magic, enchantment” appearing as an element in the name “Enchantress” (Ety/LUK). Since it ends in -th [θ], it probably developed from a primitive form such as *✶luktē̆, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/luth). This primitive form is likely the basis for its Noldorin cognate N. “spell, charm” as well, so the Doriathrin word probably has a similar meaning. The primitive [kt] would have developed into [xθ] when double voiceless stops became spirants and this simplified to [θ] when . There was a similar development for < ᴹ✶.

An Ilkorin and Doriathrin noun for “hand” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MAP, EtyAC/MAP), where the voiceless stop [p] voiced to [b] after the vowel. Since its primitive form had a short [a] and its Ilkorin form a long [ā] (EtyAC/MAP), this word is an example of how in Ilkorin.
A rejected Ilkorin name from The Etymologies from the 1930s, possibly a variation of Ilk. (EtyAC/LUY). It seems to be a combination of “hand” and the rejected form luin of “pale”.
A noun for “dough” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MASAG), where the primitive , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/maig).

An adjective meaning “soft, pliant” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/MASAG). It had essentially the same development as the noun “dough” (from ᴹ✶), because in both cases the primitive final vowel vanished without further effect.

A Doriathrin noun for “moisture” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/MIZD). The [i] lengthened due to the vocalization of [z] before voiced stops, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/míd). According to Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne, this form was originally unglossed and may have been initially intended to mean “fine rain” like its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. (EtyAC/MIZD, VTE/45).
A word for “jewel” attested only in compounds, probably of the same derivation and meaning as its Noldorin cognate N. .
A rejected and hard-to-analyze Ilkorin name for the Silmarils appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, revised to N. (EtyAC/MIR). It seems to contain “jewel”.
A noun for “night” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/MOR), where the primitive [ǭ] became [ō].

A Doriathrin noun for “sorcery”, written as mor(n)gul indicating the loss of an earlier n (Ety/ÑGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots ᴹ√ and ᴹ√. The u in the final element -gul is problematic phonetically, as it is in the similar word . Tolkien first wrote this word as morgol (EtyAC/ÑGOL), probably reflecting this phonetic uncertainty. As with , Tolkien may have resolved this uncertainty by deciding this word was Noldorin, since N. appears in a marginal note in The Etymologies (EtyAC/ÑGOL).

A Doriathrin noun for “pool”, derived from root ᴹ√ (Ety/MBOTH). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form of *✶mbottʰō. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/moth), the primitive [mb-] might be expected to have become [b-], since in Ilkorin, as for example Ilk. < MBIRÍL.
A Doriathrin adjective meaning “secret, veiled” derived from root ᴹ√ (Ety/MUY), apparently a combination of “vagueness” and the adjective-suffix -in.

The Ilkorin noun for “nightingale”, appearing as both murilind and myrilind (Ety/MOR, TIN). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form of *✶morilindē, further supported by the rejected Ilkorin form morilind (EtyAC/MOR). This would have produced murilind according to the rules of Ilkorin i-affection. The variant form myrilind hints at a different (dialectical?) phonetic development, as pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/murilind). See the entry on i-affection for further discussion.
A Doriathrin noun meaning “field, valley” (Ety/NAD), also appearing as nan and described as “land at foot of hill with many streams” (EtyAC/NAD).
An Ilkorin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, likely a combination of “valley” and the name (Ety/DAY).
A Doriathrin noun for “web” (Ety/NAT). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶natsē, where the [ts] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin word for “Dwarf” derived from the root ᴹ√NAUK- or (Ety/NAUK). Tolkien said that it was a diminutive form, not a direct cognate of ᴹQ. or N. . It may be derived from a primitive form such as *✶naukle, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/naugol), though there isn’t enough evidence to determine the original final vowel, since primitive final vowels vanished in Ilkorin. The final -ol appeared because [o] developed between a consonant and final [l] in Ilkorin.

Its form naugla appears as an element in Dor. “Necklace of the Dwarves” (Ety/NAUK).

A Doriathrin noun meaning “face” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/NIB). The vowel change suggests a primitive form *✶niba, where the [i] became [e] because of Ilkorin a-affection. If this is the case, it is not a direct cognate of N. “front, face”.

The Doriathrin number “three” attested only as an element in the word “beech” = “three trunks” (Ety/NEL). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *✶neledē, which would have become Ilk. neld due to the Ilkorin syncope, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/neldor).

A Doriathrin adjective for “wise, magical” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÑGOL, THIN). In an earlier version of this entry, the forms were ngûl and gûl, but these were rejected (EtyAC/ÑGOL). It may be that Tolkien was considering making this another case where long [ō] became [ū] in Ilkorin, but he rejected the idea. In the entry for ÑGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as both ngôl and gôl; the first of seems to be a variant of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin.

gloss: one of the wise folk, Gnome
notes: A Doriathrin name for the ᴹQ. from the same primitive root ᴹ√ÑGÓLOD (Ety/ÑGOLOD). In the entry for ÑGOLOD in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)gold, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin. The second [o] of the primitive form was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Its genitive form golda also appeared as an element in the name “*Noldo-jewel” = Silmaril.

gloss: one of the wise folk, Gnome

notes: A Doriathrin noun for “magic, lore” from the primitive root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÑGOL), most likely from the primitive form *✶ŋgolwe based on its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. . In the entry for ÑGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)golo, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [ŋg] became [g] in Ilkorin. After its final vowel was lost, the final [w] became [u], which then became [o], the only Doriathrin example of this second change.

A Doriathrin noun for “horror” derived from the root ᴹ√ÑGÓROTH (Ety/ÑGOROTH). Its Noldorin cognate N. indicates a primitive form *✶ŋgorotʰo, where the second o was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Ordinarily, an initial ng- became g- in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ngorth), and ngorth seems to be a variation on this rule.
A Doriathrin adjective meaning “horrible”, a combination of “horror” with the adjective suffix -in (Ety/ÑGOROTH).

A Doriathrin word meaning “forward” or “west”, derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/NIB). It could have developed from primitive forms like *✶nibon or *✶nibn(ǝ), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/nivon), the sense “west” probably developed from the meaning “forward” because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions.
A Doriathrin noun for “nose” derived from ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is likely an example of how , especially if the [e] first became [i] before the [ŋg], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/nîw).

An adjective meaning “hideous, horrible” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ÚLUG). Its Telerin cognate ᴹT. indicates a primitive form *✶ulgā, so that in the Ilkorin word the short [u] became [o] preceding the final [a] before that final vowel vanished.

A noun for “blood” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/YAR). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *✶yār(ǝ) [jārǝ], where the vowel changed to [o] because of Ilkorin a-affection. Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that the primitive form was *✶yara because of the Quenya stem form yar-, with a lengthening of the vowel in the primitive monosyllabic form (AL-Ilkorin/ôr) @@@ examine further.

A Doriathrin noun for “tree” derived from the root ᴹ√ÓR-NI or ᴹ√ÓRON (Ety/ÓR-NI, EtyAC/NEL). According Tolkien, it was “in Doriath used especially of beech, but as a suffix [it was] used of any tree of any size” (Ety/ÓR-NI). The root ᴹ√ÓR-NI in The Etymologies suggests a primitive form of ᴹ✶ornĭ, but elsewhere Tolkien indicated the primitive form was ᴹ✶ornē (e.g. on SD/302). Both primitive forms would have produced Ilk. orn, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orn).

A Doriathrin noun for “mountain” derived from the root ᴹ√ÓROT (Ety/ÓROT). Its Old Noldorin cognate ON. suggests a primitive form *✶orotō, where the second [o] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope [orto]. Later the [t] became [θ] (“th”) because in Ilkorin. Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orth). This word has two distinct plural forms attested: Dor. orthin (Ety/ÓROT) and Ilk. urthin (EtyAC/WATH); this could represent distinct rules for the formation of in the two dialects.
A noun for “war” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/OKTĀ). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, in this case [kt] > [xθ] (or [θθ]) > [θ].

A Doriathrin word for “east”, derived from the root ᴹ√ “back, return” (Ety/RAD). It could have developed from primitive forms like *✶radon or *✶radn(ǝ), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/radhon), the sense “east” probably developed from the meaning “back” because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions, so that East was behind them.
A Doriathrin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of “east” and “border” (Ety/RAD, RĪ).

A word meaning “flow, course of river” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RAT). It probably developed from an nasal-infixed variant of the root such *✶ranta, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rant).

A Doriathrin noun for “holly” attested only in the plural forms regin and region (Ety/ERÉK). It also appeared as an element in the word “holly-tree”. It seems that the latter word replaced reg in the singular, and the original survived only in the plurals, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/regorn).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “holly-tree”, a combination of (archaic?) “holly” and “tree” (Ety/ERÉK, ÓR-NI).
A Doriathrin variation of appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s (Ety/ÉREK). It was translated “Hollin” and appears to be the genitive plural of Ilk. “holly-tree”.

A noun meaning “a cut” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RIS²). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶ristā, where the [i] became [e] due to Ilkorin a-affection, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rest).
A Doriathrin noun for “precipice” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/KHARÁS), an example of how in Ilkorin.
A Doriathrin noun meaning “edge, hem, border” derived from the root ᴹ√RĪ (Ety/RĪ). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶rīmā, where the primitive final vowel vanished in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun meaning “cold pool or lake (in mountains)” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/RINGI). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. suggests a primitive form *✶riñgwi [riŋgwi]. This is problematic, since , as with Dor. < ᴹ✶liñ(g)wi. It is possible, though, that this word developed directly from the root form *✶riñgi [riŋgi], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ring).
A noun meaning “domed roof” derived from a nasal-infixed form of the root ᴹ√ “roof, cave” (Ety/ROD).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “plain, wide land between mountains” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/ROS²).

A Doriathrin noun for “cave”, also appearing as roth, derived from primitive ᴹ✶ or ᴹ✶roda (Ety/ROD, EtyAC/ROD). The [d] spirantilized to [ð] (“dh”) as usual, then after the final vowel was lost the as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/roth). The original sound [ð] is preserved in the plural rodhin.
A noun for “grass” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/SALÁK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin.

A noun meaning “drinking-vessel” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/SUK). This word went through a number of phonetic changes:

  • the [k] became [g] before the nasal [m]
  • the [u] shifted to [o] before the final [a]
  • the [g] vocalized to [u] before the nasal [m] producing the diphthong [ou]
  • the resulting diphthong [ou] became [au]

Helge Fauskanger originally suggested these developments (AL-Ilkorin/saum).

An adjective meaning “firm, stiff, solid” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TAK). Since it ends with “ch” [x] instead of “g”, most likely its primitive form was *✶takka, since in Ilkorin. Its middle vowel must have been a short [a], otherwise the long [ā] would have become [ō]. Therefore, this word is an example of how in Ilkorin. Both these phonetic developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger in his study of Ilkorin (AL-Ilkoring/tâch).

A verb meaning “to fix, construct, make” derived from the root ᴹ√, attested only its 3rd singular present tense form taga “he fixes, constructs, makes” (Ety/TAK). The [k] became [g] after a vowel as usual.
An adjective meaning “steep, tall, deep” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/AYAK, EtyAC/TĀ). The [k] became [g] after a vowel as usual.
A noun for “foot” derived from the ᴹ√ (Ety/TAL). It is unusual in that its plural form tel involved Ilkorin i-affection but not the suffix , as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tal).

A noun meaning “ground, floor” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TALAM). Most likely it developed from primitive *✶talama, first losing the second [a] due to the Ilkorin syncope and the final [a] when , after which the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [um]. These developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/talum).

A noun meaning “pin, brooch” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ [taŋkla] (Ety/TAK). First the [k] became [g] after the nasal [ŋ] and then final [l] became syllabic and developed into [ol]. These developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tangol).
An adjective meaning “tough, stiff” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ after primitive final vowels vanished (Ety/TÁRAG).
A noun for “pin” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TAK), where the [ks] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.

A noun meaning “holder, socket, hasp, clasp, staple” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/KUƷ). Most likely its development was similar to that of : first the [k] became [g] before the nasal, then the [g] vocalized to [u] before the [m] and finally the diphthong [ou] became [au].
A noun meaning “wood (place and material), forest” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ after primitive final vowels vanished (Ety/TÁWAR).

A noun for “silver” derived from the root ᴹ✶KYÉLEP (Ety/KYELEP), most likely from a primitive form *✶kyelepē [kjelepē]. In Ilkorin, the initial [t] developed from [kj] because , the middle [e] vanished due to the Ilkorin syncope, and the [p] became [f] because voiceless stops became spirants after liquids (like [l]). These developments were all suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/telf).

A noun meaning “close, end, last part” derived from the root ᴹ√ (EtyAC/TELES). Its Quenya cognates ᴹQ. and ᴹQ. (< ᴹ✶) suggest a primitive form of *✶telesē. The middle [e] would have vanished due to the Ilkorin syncope, after which apparently the , though this is the only example of this change.

A noun meaning “carpenter, wright, builder” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/STAB). The initial [s] spirantalized the following [t] to [θ] (“th”), while the [b] spirantalized to [v] after a vowel, and [n] became syllabic, developing into [-on] after it became final. These developments were all suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thavon).
A shorter Ilkorin name for Ilk. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s (Ety/THIN). It is simply “grey” used as a name.
An adjective for “grey” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/THIN) because primitive final vowels vanished in Ilkorin.

A noun for “pine-tree” derived from the root ᴹ√, also appearing in its genitive plural form thonion “of pines” (Ety/THŌN, EtyAC/THŌN). Helge Fauskanger suggested that it developed from primitive *✶thon- with a short ŏ because the [ō] did not become [ū] before the nasal (AL-Ilkorin/thôn), and only later did the short vowel lengthen in the monosyllable. I think that Mr. Fauskanger may have over-generalized this rule, however, since the other examples of [ō] becoming [ū] occur only before [m] and the change may not have applied to nasals in general. If this is the case, this word could have developed from primitive *✶thōn-. There is not enough evidence to say for certain either way.

Conceptual Development: In notes elsewhere this word was given the form Dor. than with genitive plural form thanion (LR/405), probably associated with the earlier name Dorthanion versus later (LR/145). It is also possible these are Doriathrin and Ilkorin variations of the same word.

A noun for “eagle” derived from the root ᴹ√THÓRON (Ety/THOR). Its cognates ᴹQ. and N. suggest a primitive form *✶thoronē, where the middle [o] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Its plural form is not thurin as printed in The Lost Road, but is actually thurnin matching its singular (EtyAC/THOR), as predicted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thorn).
Ilkorin name for N. appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, translated “King of Eagles” (Ety/THOR). It is a combination of “eagle” and “king”.

An adjective meaning “stiff, hard” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/STARAN). First the unstressed vowel in the first syllable vanished to produce the favored combination [tr], after which the initial [s] spirantalized the following [t] to [θ] (“th”), while the long [ā] became [ō]. All these developments were suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/thrôn).

A noun meaning “(starry) twilight, starlight”, a combination of “star” and “twilight” (Ety/DOMO, TIN), also appearing in its genitive form tinduma (Ety/THIN). Either the compound preserved the original [n] from tim < ᴹ✶, or the [n] reformed by assimilation to the [d].

A verb meaning “to sparkle” derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/TIN), most likely from a primitive verb *✶tinglā. If so, it is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [ŋg]. This development was pointed out by Helge Fauskanger, though he suggested the primitive verb was *✶tintilā, a cognate Q. , with a medial development of [-nt(i)l-] > [-ngl-] (AL-Ilkorin/tingla-).
An adjective meaning “thick, fat” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/TIW), where the primitive [iu] became [io] and the [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel, as was usual in Ilkorin.

A verb for “to bring” derived from the root ᴹ√, attested only in its 3rd-singular present form toga “he brings” (Ety/TUK). Here the short [u] became [o] before the final [a] and the [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/toga). The base form might be tug-.

A verb for “to fetch” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, attested only in its 3rd-singular present form tolda “he fetches” (Ety/TUK). Here the short [u] became [o] before the final [a]. The change of [lt] to [ld] is harder to explain, since ordinarily voiceless stops became spirants after liquids in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tolda).

A noun for “king” derived from primitive ᴹ✶, also appearing in its plural form tórin (Ety/TĀ, BAL). Tolkien said that it was “only used of the legitimate kings of whole tribes”, though apparently it also survived in compounds like “King of Eagles” (Ety/THOR) and “Vala-king” (Ety/BAL). It is an example of how [ā] became [ō] in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tôr).
A noun for “queen”, a combination of “king” with the feminine suffix , though according to Tolkien it was used only as a title for Melian (Ety/TĀ).
A title for appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of “king” with his name (Ety/TĀ, Ety/THIN).
A variant form of Ilk. , a combination of “king” and the genitive plural of “eagle” (Ety/THOR).
